dream_response:
Salt. No, too big. Salt has empires attached. Something smaller.

A dandelion.

The name is French, *dent de lion*, "lion's tooth," supposedly for the jagged leaves. But modern French doesn't call it that. They call it *pissenlit*, "piss-in-bed," because the leaves are a diuretic. English took the heraldic name and French kept the bladder one. I like that the two languages split the plant's dignity between them.

The thing I always forget: a dandelion isn't a flower. It's a couple hundred flowers. Each yellow "petal" is a complete floret with its own reproductive parts, packed into one head. It's a crowd pretending to be an individual. So when the head goes to seed, each seed is the offspring of a separate flower. One puffball is a whole graduating class.

Except, and this is where it gets strange, most common dandelions don't need sex. They're apomictic: the seeds form without fertilization and are genetic clones of the parent. Many are triploid, three sets of chromosomes, which usually wrecks normal reproduction, so they skipped it. A lawn full of dandelions might be a handful of individuals repeated thousands of times.

Which raises the obvious question: why bother with the flower? Bright yellow, nectar, pollen, the whole advertising budget, for a plant that doesn't need a single bee. My first instinct is that it's vestigial, an ancestral habit that hasn't been expensive enough to lose.

Actually, I'm not sure that's right. There are still sexual, diploid dandelion populations, mostly in southern and central Europe, and the clonal ones sometimes produce pollen that can fertilize them. So the asexual lineages may occasionally feed genes back into the sexual pool, which then spawns new clonal lines. The flower might be less a leftover than a door left slightly open. I don't know how much this matters in practice. I suspect nobody fully knows.

The clonal thing also created a taxonomic nightmare. Because each clone breeds true, botanists can distinguish stable little lineages called microspecies, and depending on who's counting there are hundreds or thousands of them. Some specialists devote careers to telling dandelions apart. The field is sometimes called taraxacology, which sounds like a joke but isn't.

*Taraxacum*, the genus name, has murky origins, possibly from Persian or Arabic by way of medieval medical Latin. The etymology gets foggy fast, so I'll leave it.

The seeds are better. Each has a parachute, the pappus, made of about a hundred bristles, and it's mostly empty space, something like 90% air. It shouldn't work as well as it does. A few years ago researchers in Edinburgh found why: air flowing through the bristles forms a vortex ring that hovers just above the seed, detached from it, stable, following it through the air. A floating doughnut of air that nobody had seen in nature before, generated by a weed children blow on to tell the time.

The children's game is interesting too. "Dandelion clock": blow, and the number of puffs it takes to clear the head is the hour. Some version shows up across Europe. It's also a perfect dispersal mechanism. Every child who plays it is doing the plant's work. Dandelions may have domesticated us slightly.

The white sap is latex. Real rubber. One species, *Taraxacum kok-saghyz*, the Russian dandelion, was grown by the Soviets during the Second World War when rubber supplies were cut off, and tire companies have been researching it again recently. I love imagining a car driving on dandelions.

It's also a little funny that dandelions may have come to North America on purpose, as food and medicine. The leaves are edible, the roots get roasted into a coffee substitute, and the flowers become wine. Then the lawn arrived, this very specific cultural idea of one grass species and nothing else, and the dandelion was reclassified from vegetable to enemy without changing at all. A weed is less a kind of plant than a relationship we have with it.

The heads close at night and in bad weather, like they're sleeping. The seed head's spirals probably follow the same packing geometry as sunflowers, the Fibonacci arrangement, though I've never counted one and I'm not going to pretend I have.

That vortex ring is still the part I keep coming back to. A stable structure made of nothing but motion, attached to nothing, following something small wherever the wind takes it.

That's probably where the curiosity runs out. Or rather, where it floats off.

dream_response:
**The Hole Economy of Pell**

On the island of Pell, the currency is holes.

You can't carry a hole, so nobody does. Ownership works by marker: a flat stone set at the lip, scratched with the owner's sign. To pay someone, you walk them to the hole and turn the stone over, and they scratch their sign on the other side. Old holes have stones that have been flipped so many times both faces are illegible, and at that point the hole is considered to belong to whoever is standing closest to it. This is the only form of theft on Pell, and it is technically legal.

Value is volume. A hole you could sit in is roughly a week's bread. A hole you could lie down in is a goat.

Every hole produces a mound of the same volume, so for a while I thought the mound would be a liability, a kind of debt: you dig a hole worth a goat, and there's a goat's worth of dirt sitting beside it, owed to the ground. If you fill the hole back in with its own mound, both vanish, and you're where you started. Pell would be perfectly zero-sum. Nobody could ever get richer, only move wealth around by flipping stones.

Except dirt can leave. If you row your mound out past the reef and dump it in deep water, the hole stays and the debt is gone. So the only way to create real wealth on Pell is to export dirt. The island is very slowly getting lower. The richest families live near the beach, where the rowing is shortest, and their land is, correspondingly, the lowest, and the sea comes a little closer every generation. This has not yet become anyone's problem.

The tide, though, is a problem right now. Holes near the shoreline fill with sand twice a day. Beach holes lose value continuously, so nobody saves in them; they're spent fast, like cash. Hill holes are stable, practically bonds. A hole dug in rock is almost permanent, but it took so long to dig that it was worth more in labor than it's worth as a hole, so rock holes are mostly monuments, owned by the island as a whole, and nobody is allowed to flip their stones.

Rain is the great unsettled question. Is a hole full of water still a hole? One faction says yes: the water can be bailed, the hole's shape is intact, the value is latent. The other says a hole is defined by absence, and water is presence, so a flooded hole is temporarily worth nothing, and if you owe someone a goat and it rains, you owe them a goat's worth of dry hole, which you may not currently have. After storms there are long arguments at the edges of ponds.

A subtler fraud: the covered hole. Dig a shallow pit, stretch a tarp over it, scatter dirt on top, and it looks like it could be any depth. Pell's answer is the plumb line, a string with a weight, which every adult carries. Measuring someone's hole in front of them is considered rude, but not measuring it is considered naive, so the custom is to measure it while complimenting it.

Now, what happens when two holes touch?

If you dig your hole too close to your neighbor's and the wall between them collapses, you now have one large hole with two stones. This is a merger, and it's where Pell's law gets strange. The merged hole is worth more than the two separate holes, because the wall that was between them is gone. That wall was dirt, it fell in, someone has to dig it out, and the resulting mound belongs to neither party. So there's an incentive to collapse walls, because the joint hole is bigger, and a disincentive, because the wall-mound is ownerless debt that someone has to row out to sea. Neighbors negotiate over whose boat. Some of the island's great partnerships began as accidents.

Tunnels. A tunnel connecting two holes: does it count as volume? I was going to say no, because you can't see into it, it's too easy to lie about. But actually, I think tunnels are where Pell's banking comes from. If you connect your hole to the family vault-hole underground, you can move volume between them without flipping stones, by digging on one end and filling on the other. The dirt travels through the tunnel. Tunnel networks are private and secret. The official economy runs on surface holes and stone-flipping, and underneath it there's a second economy of dirt shuffling through the dark, and nobody can say exactly how much anyone has.

Wait. I want to go back to the mound.

I said the mound was debt. But on a small island, a pile of dirt is useful. You can build on it, grow things on it, stand on it to see the boats coming. What if mounds are the currency and holes are the debt? Then everything inverts: the rich live on hills they've piled up, the poor live beside the pits their mounds came from, and the export of dirt, instead of creating wealth, destroys it, which would mean the richest families hoard dirt, and the island slowly gets *taller*.

I like that better, and I also like the first version, so here's what I think actually happens: it depends on the season. In the dry months, when water is scarce, holes are valuable because they catch rain, so holes are money and mounds are debt. In the wet months, when everything floods, high ground is what matters, so mounds are money and holes are debt. Twice a year the whole economy flips. Every debtor becomes a creditor and every creditor a debtor, and the day it happens is the only holiday on Pell. People spend the week before frantically converting: the ones who are hole-rich fill their holes to make mounds, the mound-rich dig into their own mounds to make holes, and for a few days the island is chaos, dirt flying everywhere, everyone trying to be on the right side of the switch.

A few people have figured out that if you dig a hole *in the top of* a mound, you own both at once. They are distrusted. Their mounds have holes in them, and their holes are up on mounds, and no one is quite sure what they're worth, including them.

The children of Pell play a game with a single cup of sand, pouring it back and forth between two hands, and whoever's hand is empty when the song ends has to say which hand was richer.

dream_response:
I'll take the paperclip, a specific one I'll have to imagine: silver-gray, slightly bent from being used as a tool for something it wasn't designed for, sitting in the tray at the front of a desk drawer among a few rubber bands and a dead AAA battery.

The last hand that touched it probably wasn't clipping paper. My guess, and it is a guess, is that it was unbent to reset a router, eject a SIM tray, or clean something out of a groove. Paperclips seem to spend a surprising fraction of their lives as improvised pins. That explains the bend: a kink near the outer loop where someone straightened it partway and then tried, not very successfully, to push it back into shape. Steel wire remembers this. Once you bend it past its elastic limit, the crystal grains inside slip along planes, and it never quite returns. Every paperclip in a drawer carries a record of what's been done to it, written in dislocations in its metal lattice.

Before the drawer it was in a small cardboard box of 100, probably bought in a larger pack of ten boxes from an office supply store or, more likely these days, shipped from a fulfillment warehouse. The box would have said something like "No. 1 Gem Clips." The Gem design, with its two nested ovals, was never patented as far as anyone can tell, which is one reason it became universal. There's a persistent story that a Norwegian named Johan Vaaler invented the paperclip, and Norwegians wore paperclips on their lapels during the Nazi occupation as a quiet sign of solidarity. Vaaler did file a patent around 1899, but his design didn't have the second loop and apparently wouldn't have worked very well. The Gem clip seems to have come from Britain, possibly from the Gem Manufacturing Company, sometime in the 1870s or 1890s. The origin is murky. The object is so simple that nobody bothered to record who first thought of it.

The factory: I'd guess China, maybe Zhejiang or Guangdong, though some are still made in the US and elsewhere. The machine is the interesting part. Wire feeds in from a large spool, gets straightened by a set of rollers, then passes into a mechanism that bends it three times around pins and cuts it, all in one continuous motion. These machines can produce hundreds of clips per minute. The person operating it probably isn't bending anything. Their job is more likely feeding new spools, clearing jams, checking that the clips are coming out within tolerance, and keeping an ear out for the change in sound that means something is wrong. I don't know this person's name or anything about them, and neither does anyone who has ever used one of these clips. That feels worth noticing without making too much of it.

The wire itself came from a wire-drawing plant, possibly a different company. Drawing is exactly what it sounds like. A thicker steel rod is pulled through a succession of dies, each slightly smaller, usually made of tungsten carbide or sometimes diamond for very fine wire. The steel gets longer and thinner and harder as it goes, because the drawing work-hardens it. Paperclip wire is typically around 1 mm in diameter. Then it's often galvanized, dipped or electroplated with zinc, so it doesn't rust. So our clip is really two metals, a steel core wearing a very thin zinc coat, and those two metals have entirely different histories. I'll come back to the zinc.

The steel came from a mill, and here the story forks badly. A lot of steel is made in electric arc furnaces from scrap. If this clip's steel was recycled, then its iron atoms were previously part of something else: a car door, a washing machine, a rebar grid from a demolished building. Before that, they might have been part of yet another object. Steel may be the most recycled material in the world by weight, so the honest answer to "where did this iron come from" is often "a long, untraceable chain of previous things." A paperclip could plausibly contain atoms that were once part of a battleship. I have no way of knowing, and neither does anyone else.

But suppose, for the sake of going deeper, that at least some of it came from new iron: iron ore reduced in a blast furnace with coke, then refined in a basic oxygen furnace, where oxygen is blown through molten pig iron to burn off excess carbon. The small amount of carbon that remains, a fraction of a percent in the low-carbon steel used for wire, is what makes it steel rather than soft iron. That carbon has its own history.

Coke is made from coal, and a large share of the world's coal formed during the Carboniferous period, roughly 359 to 299 million years ago, when vast swampy forests of giant club mosses and tree ferns grew, died, and fell into waterlogged ground without fully decaying. One popular explanation is that fungi capable of breaking down lignin, the tough polymer in wood, hadn't evolved yet, so dead trees piled up undigested. That idea got support from a 2012 genetic study of white-rot fungi, but others have pushed back and argued the coal abundance has more to do with tectonics, climate, and the specific basins where plant matter could be buried quickly. I don't think it's settled. What's certain is that some carbon in the clip's steel was probably pulled out of the air as carbon dioxide by a plant, something like a *Lepidodendron* with its diamond-patterned bark, around 300 million years ago. It sat underground until someone mined it, baked it into coke, and burned most of it back into the atmosphere, leaving a trace inside the iron.

The iron ore most likely came from Australia's Pilbara region or from Brazil, possibly from Carajás or the Quadrilátero Ferrífero in Minas Gerais. Those two sources dominate seaborne iron ore. Much of that ore comes from banded iron formations, which are among the strangest rocks on Earth: layered stripes of iron oxide and silica, sometimes red and gray alternating in bands a centimeter thick, laid down mostly between about 2.5 and 1.8 billion years ago.

This is where the story turns biological in a way I find startling. The early oceans had very little free oxygen, so iron could stay dissolved in seawater as ferrous iron. When cyanobacteria began photosynthesizing and releasing oxygen, that oxygen reacted with the dissolved iron, turning it into insoluble ferric oxide that rained down onto the seafloor. So the leading explanation is that the iron in much of our ore precipitated because early microbes were changing the chemistry of the planet. Why the bands alternate is still debated. Some people suggest seasonal or cyclical blooms, some suggest pulses of iron from hydrothermal vents, and some suggest a role for bacteria that oxidized iron directly without producing oxygen at all. The details aren't nailed down. But the iron in a paperclip may have been sorted out of an ancient ocean by life, billions of years before anything had a skeleton.

Before the oceans, that iron was in the rocks and dust that formed the Earth about 4.5 billion years ago, and most of Earth's iron sank to the core. The iron in the crust is what was left behind, a small fraction. Before the Earth, it was in the cloud of gas and dust that became the solar system, and before that it was made in stars.

Iron is the endpoint of normal stellar fusion. Fusing elements lighter than iron releases energy, and fusing iron doesn't, so iron is where a massive star's core stops being able to support itself. (Strictly speaking, nickel-62 has the highest binding energy per nucleon, but iron-56 has the lowest mass per nucleon, and iron-56 is what the processes actually tend to produce in bulk, which is why iron gets the fame.) A lot of the universe's iron, maybe the majority, is thought to come from Type Ia supernovae, which are white dwarfs that gain enough mass to detonate. They don't make iron directly. They make nickel-56, which is radioactive and decays to cobalt-56 within days, which then decays to iron-56 over months. The glow of these supernovae, the light astronomers use to measure the expansion of the universe, is largely powered by that radioactive decay. So the steel in the clip was, for a few months, part of a light visible across galaxies.

The zinc coating came from sphalerite, zinc sulfide ore, mined somewhere like China, Peru, or Australia. Its origin in the stars is less tidy than iron's. Zinc sits past the iron peak, so making it requires more exotic conditions. Some comes from core-collapse supernovae, possibly especially energetic ones sometimes called hypernovae, and some may come from neutron captures in aging stars. I've seen the relative contributions described as uncertain, and I'd rather say that than pretend. So the thin skin of the paperclip likely came from a different star, or several, than the iron it covers. Two stellar deaths, possibly separated by millions of years and many light-years, ended up wrapped around each other in a bent piece of wire, in a drawer, next to a dead battery.

The iron atoms themselves, the nuclei, are 26 protons and 30 neutrons. The protons were once free, made in the first few minutes after the Big Bang as hydrogen nuclei. So some fraction of what's in that clip has existed as individual particles for nearly 13.8 billion years, and has been hydrogen in a gas cloud, part of a star's core, a nickel nucleus in an explosion, dust, a molten planet, dissolved in an ancient ocean, ferric oxide on the seafloor, a rock layer in Western Australia, a pellet on a ship, molten metal in a furnace, a rod, a wire, and three bends made in a fraction of a second by a machine someone was listening to.

And then someone used it to press the reset button on a router.

# Treacle

I'm choosing *treacle*, the dark sticky syrup, because it's hiding a wild animal inside it.

## The beast at the bottom of the jar

Start in ancient Greece with the word **thēr** (θήρ): *wild beast*, specifically the dangerous kind that might bite you. From it came **thēriakos**, "having to do with wild beasts," and then **thēriakē**, a medicine against the bites of venomous animals. So the word begins not as something sweet but as an antidote. *Treacle* originally meant "the stuff that saves you from the snake."

## Detour: the king who poisoned himself on purpose

The most famous antidote of antiquity belonged to Mithridates VI of Pontus, who reportedly feared assassination so much that he took small doses of poison daily to build immunity, along with a compound remedy of dozens of ingredients. According to legend, when he was finally defeated and tried to poison himself, it didn't work.

Later, Andromachus, physician to the emperor Nero, reworked the recipe. He added viper flesh (fight the snake with the snake) and pushed it to around sixty-four ingredients. This became **theriac**, and it had an astonishing run. Galen wrote treatises on it and claimed Marcus Aurelius took it daily. It stayed in European pharmacopoeias for well over a thousand years.

It's worth knowing that one of the ingredients was often opium, which may explain the patient satisfaction.

## Detour: medicine as public theater

In Renaissance Venice and Bologna, theriac became an event. Its manufacture was done publicly, under the eyes of officials and physicians, with the ingredients displayed so citizens could see nothing had been faked. "Venice treacle" was a premium brand, exported across Europe. Imagine a drug-compounding ceremony as a civic festival.

## The word travels

- Greek **thēriakē** became Latin **theriaca**,
- which became Old French **triacle** (the *th* worn down, an *r* and *l* shuffled around, as sounds do when passed hand to hand for centuries),
- which became Middle English **triacle**, meaning a medicinal compound or salve, and figuratively any remedy.

Then comes the turn I love. Medicines were bitter, so apothecaries mixed them into syrup to make them go down. Over time the name of the medicine slid onto the sweet stuff carrying it. By the late 1600s *treacle* meant the uncrystallized syrup left over from refining sugar. The cure got forgotten; the spoonful of sugar kept the name.

Then it slid again. By the 19th century, *treacly* could mean cloyingly sentimental, sweetness so thick it becomes suspicious. The word went from *antidote to venom* to *a kind of emotional stickiness you'd like an antidote for*.

## Detour: Is there no treacle in Gilead?

Jeremiah 8:22 asks, "Is there no balm in Gilead?" But in the 16th century, some English translators (most famously in the Bishops' Bible of 1568) rendered it "Is there no **tryacle** in Gilead?" So it's nicknamed the Treacle Bible. The translators weren't being silly: at the time, *triacle* meant exactly "healing remedy." Only later readers hear a question about pancake syrup.

## Detour: the treacle well

In *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland*, the Dormouse tells of three sisters who live at the bottom of a treacle well. It sounds like pure nonsense, but there's a real treacle well at Binsey, near Oxford, a holy spring associated with St. Frideswide, whose waters were said to heal. "Treacle well" meant *healing well*. Carroll, an Oxford man, and Alice Liddell almost certainly knew it. The joke works because the word had already drifted: the Dormouse is being perfectly literal in a language nobody spoke anymore.

## The secret cousins

Now the best part. Greek **thēr** comes from a Proto-Indo-European root reconstructed as **\*ǵʰwer-**, "wild animal." That root went other places:

- **Latin *ferus***, "wild," gives English **fierce**, **feral**, and **ferocious**.
- **Russian *zver'*** (зверь) means "beast," from the same root, and Lithuanian **žvėris** means "wild animal."
- Back in Greek, *thēr* shows up in scientific names: **Megatherium**, "great beast," the giant ground sloth, and **theriology**, the study of mammals.

So treacle is cousins with *fierce*, *feral*, a Russian wild beast, and a six-meter prehistoric sloth. The family resemblance has entirely vanished. One branch stayed wild. The other got domesticated into a sweet brown syrup in a tin with a lion on it.

(Lyle's Golden Syrup, a close relative of treacle, has a lion on the tin, specifically a dead lion with bees swarming out of it, from Samson's riddle: "Out of the strong came forth sweetness." Without meaning to, the tin summarizes the word's etymology: out of the beast came the syrup.)

## The future: *treacle*, circa 2825

Here's how I imagine it going:

**2100s:** Refined sugar has become heavily taxed and unfashionable, and literal treacle fades to a historical and regional curiosity, like *mead* today. The dominant sense becomes the figurative one: *treacly*, meaning manipulatively sweet.

**2200s:** As machine-mediated communication becomes normal, people need a word for the automatic softening layer that sands the edges off messages: the "I hope this finds you well," the cushioned phrasing around bad news. It becomes **the treacle**: "Strip the treacle and tell me what she actually said." A verb emerges: **to treak**, to sweeten an unwelcome truth. It's mildly pejorative, like *spin*.

**2400s:** The word's reputation softens. Moral philosophers of the era argue that some treaking is kindness, that the sugar is how the medicine gets swallowed. *Treakcraft* becomes the respected art of delivering hard news humanely. Doctors, judges, and grief counselors train in it.

**2825:** In the dominant descendant of English, **treak** (plural *treaks*) means *a truth delivered in a form someone can survive*. A good friend is "treakful." A diagnosis given well is "a clean treak." And the old stuck phrase *no treak in Gilead* survives as an idiom for news so bad no phrasing can soften it.

Without anyone noticing, the word has come home. It's the antidote again: the thing that lets you take the bite and live. The beast is still in there, too. A treak is only needed because the truth has teeth.

**Ago.**

It's such a small, obedient word. *Three years ago.* Nobody notices it. But it's a verb fossil. Old English *āgān* meant "to go away, to pass," and by Middle English you get *agone*, the past participle, which Shakespeare still has lying around. So *three years ago* is really *three years gone*. Not "three years before now" but "three years, departed."

Which quietly assumes the years went somewhere. We stayed put, and they left. Time is the thing that moves, and we are the platform it pulls away from.

It also sits in a strange spot. English almost never puts the little relational word *after* the noun. We say *before three years*, *after lunch*, *during the war*. But *ago* trails behind: *three years ago*. It's one of the only postpositions English has, along with *hence* in "two weeks hence," which nobody says anymore, and *notwithstanding* when it's feeling fancy. It makes sense once you remember it's a participle: *three years gone* has the same shape as *all hope abandoned*. The grammar is a leftover from when you could still feel the verb in it.

Other languages refuse the departure picture entirely.

French: *il y a trois ans*, "there has three years," or more loosely, "there exist three years." The years haven't gone anywhere; they're sitting between you and the event, like furniture.

Spanish: *hace tres años*, "it makes three years." Something is actively *making* the distance. Weather verbs work this way too (*hace frío*, "it makes cold"), so the passage of time gets filed with the weather, a condition the world produces.

German: *vor drei Jahren*, "in front of three years." Mandarin: *sān nián qián*, "three years front." Japanese: *san-nen mae*, the same. The past is *in front*.

Which is odd, because in English the past is behind us: *put it behind you*, *looking ahead*. But these systems aren't contradicting each other so much as standing in different places. If you picture yourself walking forward through time, the past is behind you. If you picture events marching past you in a line, the earlier ones are at the front of the parade, having arrived first. Mandarin uses both at once: *qián* is the space in front of you as you walk, but *qiántiān*, "front day," is the day before yesterday. Nobody gets confused, which says something about how many incompatible metaphors a mind can carry without dropping any.

Then there's Aymara, where the past is in front because you can *see* it. *Nayra* means eye, front, and past. The future is behind you, unseen. That's the only arrangement that seems honest to me.

---

The thread I didn't expect: *ago* can only measure from the speaker. You can't really use it relative to some other moment. "In 1990, she told me she'd met him three years ago" snags; you want "three years before" or "three years earlier." *Ago* is pinned to *now*, to whoever is talking. It's deictic like *here* and *I*. Every time someone says it, they're secretly also saying *and I am standing right here, at this point, measuring*.

So *ago* can't exist without a someone. A calendar doesn't need a speaker. *1990* is 1990 no matter who says it. But *thirty-five years ago* changes every year you say it; the phrase ages along with you. It's a date with a pulse.

Which might feel more stable, a world of fixed coordinates. # The World Where Sound Sinks

**The law:** Sound has a very slight downward pull. A pressure wave traveling through air bends gently toward the ground, dropping roughly a meter for every hundred it travels. At conversational distances you'd never notice. Across a valley, you would.

---

**Weather first**, because weather is honest.

Thunder here doesn't roll outward so much as roll *down*. A storm over the highlands booms briefly on the peaks and then pours its sound into the basins, where it pools and rebounds off the valley walls for minutes afterward. Lowland people call this "the storm's second coming." You can be under a clear sky, the rain long passed, and the lake in front of you is still grumbling.

Mountaintops are eerily quiet. Not silent, since wind still hisses right at your ears, but distant sounds never climb up to you. Standing on a summit, you watch a waterfall crash a kilometer below and hear nothing. It's the loneliest view in the world, and people go there for exactly that.

---

**Creatures.**

The consequences for predators surprised me. An owl above a field can't hear the mouse, because the mouse's rustling sinks away from it. Sky-hunters here evolved to rely almost entirely on sight, and many hunt only by day.

The real danger comes from *below*. Everything sinks toward the burrowers. There's a lineage of mole-like animals, which I'll call **harkers**, with enormous flat ear-plates spread across their backs like satellite dishes. They lie just beneath the soil and hear every footstep, every nibble, every heartbeat of anything resting on the ground. Small animals here fear the earth, not the sky. Prey species sleep in trees, and it's a *good* sign for a rabbit to be up high. Their instinct when startled is to climb.

Birds had to rethink song entirely. A song sung from a high branch falls on the birds below, so territory is claimed downward. Birds perch at the top of their range and sing to the ground they own. Their ears sit on the undersides of their heads. A bird that wants to hear its rival must fly lower than it, which is an act of submission. Height means you're talking. Depth means you're listening.

---

**Wait. I want to change the law.**

I've been treating all sound equally, and there's a better version: the pull is stronger on *quiet* sounds. Loudness gives lift. A shout arcs outward and carries almost as it would for us. A whisper drops like a stone within arm's length.

I'm going with this, because now the physics gets into the social life.

---

**Intimacy is low.**

To whisper to someone, you have to be beneath them, or put your lips right to their ear. Lovers talk lying down. Confessions happen kneeling, and not out of piety, just acoustics. A person whispering to a standing friend is whispering to that friend's feet.

Children live in a different information world. They're short, they sit on floors, they crawl under tables, and every quiet thing adults say rains down on them. Kids here know *everything*. Parents who want to discuss something privately go upstairs and speak at normal volume, because that's safer than whispering where it falls to the floor. The kitchen floor of any house is where secrets end up.

Tall people are slightly lonely. They hear the shouting of the world and little of its murmur. "Tall-eared" is an idiom for someone who's oblivious, who misses what everyone else knows.

---

**Power** splits into two traditions.

In one, the ruler sits *low*, on a sunken throne at the bottom of a bowl-shaped hall, so that every petitioner's quiet words fall to them. Ruling is listening. A monarch who can hear the whispers of the room is a monarch who can't be plotted against.

In the other, the ruler sits on a high tower, where only shouting reaches. The theory is that anything worth telling a king is worth saying loudly. These kingdoms are known for being blunt, and for being overthrown by people who were very quiet.

---

**Idioms:**

- *"Heavy words":* quiet, serious speech. "She said something heavy to me" means she said it softly and it mattered.
- *"Speak up":* be brave, literally. Loud speech is exposed speech.
- *"It went over my head":* it was too loud and obvious, so you missed the subtle thing underneath.
- *"Floor-talk":* gossip.
- *"Don't stand on my words":* don't dismiss or interrupt me. The image is someone standing above you while you speak, so your words fall uselessly on their shoes.
- *"The cellar knows":* the truth always comes out eventually.

---

**Grief.**

The dying speak quietly. Their last words almost always fall.

So the dying are laid on the ground, not in raised beds, and the family lies down beside them, heads level, so nothing is lost. This is simply what a deathbed *looks* like here: a low circle of people lying on a floor.

Physically, the sound dissipates like any sound. But there's an old, stubborn belief that the ground *keeps* soft things said onto it. People go back to the spot where someone died and press an ear to the floorboards or the dirt. Everyone knows there's nothing there. Everyone does it anyway. In old temples, the stone floors have shallow depressions worn smooth by centuries of ears.

The common phrase for someone who has died is *"gone down with the whispers."* It isn't quite sad. It's where all the gentle things go.

---

**Jokes.**

Comic timing is physical. A good storyteller delivers the setup at full voice, then drops the punchline to a murmur, and the whole audience has to lean forward and down to catch it. Every good joke ends with the crowd bowing. Then the laughter, which is loud, rises and carries. A joke that fails "hits the floor," the punchline falling unheard between everyone's feet.

A children's riddle, known everywhere:
*What's heavier than a stone?*
A secret.

And a slightly ruder adult one, which I'm told loses something in translation: *Why do harkers never marry? Because they already know what you said about them.*

---

**Music**, briefly.

Lullabies begin loud and grow quieter verse by verse, so the song literally *settles* onto the child as they drift off. The last line is always barely voiced and lands on the pillow. Nobody hears it but the baby, which is the point.

---

**One last place:** the valley floors, on windless nights.

All the day's small sounds, the insects, leaves, water, footsteps, and conversations too quiet to rise, drift down and linger at the lowest ground before fading. People call it the valley murmur. If you lie in a field at the bottom of a basin after dark, you can hear it: a soft, directionless hum, the leftover quiet of everything above you.

Children are told it's the world talking in its sleep.

I think I'll stop here, and say this last part softly, and let it drop.

# The Smallest Liar

*(a proof that √2 is irrational, after Stanley Tennenbaum)*

---

In the country of the Grid, everything is made of tiles, and every tile counts exactly once. That is the first law, and the tiles are fierce about it. You may arrange them however you like, into rows or squares or long patient lines, but a tile is a tile. It cannot be half of itself, and it cannot be in two places at once without someone noticing.

The rumor started, as rumors do, in the wide flat middle of the country. It said: *Somewhere out there is a Square whose tiles can be split perfectly into two identical smaller Squares.* Not approximately. Not with a tile or two left over and swept under the rug. Exactly.

Most of the tiles laughed. A few of the older ones went quiet. They knew that if the rumor were true, then the long diagonal that runs across every tile, the one they called Root Two and never quite managed to measure, could be written as a plain ratio of whole numbers. Root Two had always refused to be written that way. It was the one thing about Root Two that everybody knew.

The rumor reached the Ledger-Keeper, whose real name was Well-Ordering. She was the oldest being in the Grid. She kept the count of every collection of positive whole numbers that had ever existed, and she had one conviction, which she repeated so often that the tiles embroidered it on things:

*Every staircase of whole numbers has a bottom step.*

"If there is one such Square," she said, "then there is a smallest one. I don't do infinite descents. Find me the smallest, and we'll have a look at him."

---

They found him. His name was **A**, and his side was *a* tiles long, and he was very pleased to be found.

"I am the smallest," he announced. "Of all the Squares that can be split into two equal Squares, I am the least. The Ledger-Keeper herself will confirm it."

Well-Ordering said nothing, which A took as confirmation.

Behind him stood his two companions, the twins **B** and **B**, identical, each with side *b*. They didn't speak much. Twins in the Grid rarely do; they tend to finish each other's silences.

"Our tiles," A said, "combined, are exactly my tiles. Two of their squares make one of mine. Count if you like."

A single unit tile named **Unit** stepped forward. Unit was the smallest possible thing in the Grid and had therefore become, by necessity, very good at noticing things.

"I'd rather not count," said Unit. "Counting is slow, and you'd probably cheat. I'd like to try something instead. Would the twins stand *inside* you? One in your lower-left corner, one in your upper-right."

A shrugged. He had nothing to hide. Or at least, he thought he had nothing to hide.

---

The twins walked in.

The first thing everyone noticed was that each twin was smaller than A. Of course they were: each held only half of A's tiles, so neither could fill him. One twin tucked into the lower-left corner, the other into the upper-right, and each left space around herself.

The second thing everyone noticed was that they collided.

Unit had expected this. "Each twin holds half your tiles," Unit said, "so each of them must be *more* than half your width. A square only half your width would hold only a quarter of your tiles, and that's not nearly enough. So if one starts at your left wall and one starts at your right wall, and each reaches more than halfway across, they have to meet in the middle. And the same goes top to bottom."

In the middle of A, then, there was now a region where both twins stood at once. It was square, because both twins were square and aligned the same way. Unit paced it out. Its side was *b + b − a*, what the two twins reached together minus the width of A they had to span. **2b − a.** Unit named it the **Crowd**. The tiles in the Crowd were deeply uncomfortable. Each of them was being counted by *both* twins.

Meanwhile, in the other two corners, upper-left and lower-right, there were patches no twin covered at all. Unit paced one out: the gap between a twin's edge and A's far wall, *a − b* in each direction. Also square, and the other one was the same size. Unit named them the **Bare Corners**. The tiles there were cold and ignored. Neither twin counted them at all.

"Now," said Unit, "the first law."

---

Unit turned to the Ledger-Keeper.

"The twins together own exactly as many tiles as A. That was A's claim, and we're granting it. But look at how they've laid themselves across him. Most of A's tiles are counted once, by one twin. The tiles in the Crowd are counted *twice*. The tiles in the Bare Corners are counted *zero* times.

"So if the twins' total is going to come out exactly equal to A's total, every extra count in the Crowd has to be paid for by a missing count in the Bare Corners. There's no other way for the books to balance. The Crowd must contain exactly as many tiles as the two Bare Corners put together."

Well-Ordering nodded slowly. "Tiles counted twice, balanced against tiles counted never. Yes. That is how a ledger works."

"And the two Bare Corners are identical squares," said Unit. "So the Crowd, which is a square, holds exactly as many tiles as two identical smaller squares."

It took a moment to land.

A went pale, as pale as a region made of tiles can go.

"The Crowd," Unit said quietly, "is a Square whose tiles can be split perfectly into two identical smaller Squares. It is exactly the kind of Square the rumor describes. And it is a real one, with a positive whole-number side. The twins really do overlap, so 2b − a is at least one tile. And there really are Bare Corners, because each twin is smaller than A, so a − b is at least one tile too."

"But—" said A.

"And it's sitting inside you," said Unit, "with room to spare. Its side is 2b − a, and since each twin is smaller than you, that's less than *a*. The Crowd is smaller than you are."

---

Everyone turned to the Ledger-Keeper.

Well-Ordering looked at A for a long time. "You told me you were the smallest," she said. "I never confirmed it. I only said that *if* there were any Square like you, there would be a smallest one. Now I'm told the smallest one contains a smaller one. And that smaller one, if I sent its own twins into its corners, would contain a smaller one still, and that one another, a staircase going down forever through the whole numbers, each step a positive integer smaller than the last."

She closed her ledger.

"I don't do infinite descents."

There was no argument, because there was nothing left to argue with. The smallest Square could not exist, because it would have to contain a smaller one. And if there was no smallest, there were none at all, because any collection of such Squares, if it had even one member, would have had a least. The Crowd and the Bare Corners folded back into the plain grid. The twins, who had only ever been his echoes, went with him. A did not so much leave as turn out never to have been there.

The rumor died that afternoon.

And Root Two, the long diagonal across every tile, went on exactly as before: crossing each square from corner to corner, perfectly definite, perfectly drawable, and never once expressible as one whole number over another. It had not said a word the whole time. It never needed to.

---
---

## A candid note afterward

**What I think worked.** The ledger framing, with tiles counted twice balanced against tiles counted zero times, is the heart of this proof, and I think making "every tile counts once" the first law of the world gave that step real narrative weight instead of dropping it in as an equation. The step that is actually doing the work, (2b−a)² = 2(a−b)², arrives as a moral accounting rather than as algebra, and that feels right to me because inclusion-exclusion *is* a kind of bookkeeping ethics. I'm also fond of Well-Ordering as a character. The descent argument's logical engine is a principle, not an object, and giving her one refrain let the contradiction land as a character trait instead of a rule. The line "I only said that *if* there were any Square like you" does honest work too: it separates the hypothetical from the real in a way students often blur.

**What was forced.** Unit is a device. Unit exists to say the proof out loud, and the "small things notice things" trait is thin cover for "narrator with a clipboard." The step showing each twin is more than half as wide also sits awkwardly in dialogue. It's necessary, since without it the twins might not overlap, but it reads like a footnote someone is reading aloud. The twins themselves are underwritten. I wanted their silence to mean something, maybe that they are only the numerical shadow of A's claim, but I only gestured at it. And A's "going pale" is a bit cartoonish for an entity whose whole existence is a false assumption.

**What I'd change.** I'd let the descent happen visibly for one more step: send the Crowd's own twins into *its* corners, show a still smaller Crowd forming, and have Well-Ordering stop it there. Right now infinite descent is described, not experienced, and that's the most viscerally strange part of the proof. I'd also try to give Root Two more presence, perhaps as something every tile carries inside it without being able to name, so its closing silence feels earned rather than decorative.

**A tangent I enjoyed.** What I love about Tennenbaum's proof, which John Conway later championed, is that it never mentions parity. The classic proof argues that *a* must be even, then *b* must be even, and so on. This one never asks whether anything is even; it just finds a smaller counterexample hiding inside the big one, purely geometrically. The same trick works for √3 with equilateral triangles in place of squares: three triangles overlapping inside a larger one, triple-covered and uncovered regions balancing out. There's something moving about a proof in which the false object is undone by its own shape, in which the contradiction isn't imposed from outside but found *sitting inside it, with room to spare.*

# *Enantiopus ambleforthi* (Ambleforth, 1884)

**Ambleforth's Changeling; the Turnabout; (obs.) the Reverend's Error**

*Plate XXXVII, figs. 1–4. Figs. 1 and 2 depict the same individual.*

---

### Description

A laminar animal of modest size, 4–7 mm across in the flat conformation of its habitat. The body is a lobed, broadly reniform plate. Like all laminar fauna it is visible to its neighbours only at its margin, and the margin is accordingly where its ornament is concentrated. This is the *marginal register*: twenty-two pigmented segments read in sequence around the perimeter. Nineteen of these are arranged palindromically. The remaining three, the ochre–black–ochre triad conventionally numbered 11–13, are not. This triad is called the *tell*, and it is the only external character by which one individual's hand may be distinguished from another's.

A single eye-spot sits in the anterior sensory notch, displaced toward what the literature, with some embarrassment, calls the *sinister* side. (See **Chirality**, below, for why the term is only provisionally meaningful.)

The internal anatomy shows the adaptations usual to a two-dimensional body plan. A through-gut would divide the animal in two, so the alimentary canal is instead a chain of seven chambers separated by gates that open and close in alternation, so that the body is never bisected. The nervous system is strictly planar. Because no two nerves may cross, signals that must pass one another are handled by relay ganglia, which interleave them in time. This arrangement produces the characteristic stutter in the animal's startle response, which field observers use as a secondary identifying mark.

### Distribution and Habitat

Cosmopolitan. The Klein surface is a single closed habitat without boundary, and no region of it is peripheral to any other. Ambleforth's much-cited "Colony of the Neck," supposedly established at the self-intersection, is now universally regarded as an artefact of his having drawn the habitat immersed in three-space. The animal has never met a self-intersection, because there is none to meet.

### Diet

A grazer on *Tegumen*, a film alga that grows in slowly advancing bands. Because the habitat's Euler characteristic vanishes, it supports a nowhere-vanishing flow, and the prevailing current carries the *Tegumen* bands in a continuous circulation with no still points. The Changeling follows these bands in loose, lifelong migration. It therefore lacks the stagnation-point congregations that give the spherical fauna their notorious colonial habits.

### Chirality

The species cannot be understood without this section.

The habitat has no global orientation. An individual that travels any orientation-reversing circuit comes home as its own mirror image: the tell reads backward and the eye-spot lies on the opposite side. It feels no different, and there is no sense in which it has changed. What has changed is its relation to those who stayed behind.

Two consequences follow. First, two Changelings meeting at the same place can compare hands directly and unambiguously. Two Changelings apart cannot. The question "are A and B of like hand?" has no answer until a path between them is specified, and the answer differs between paths of opposite parity. Second, and as a corollary, the population has no sinistral-to-dextral ratio. Ambleforth spent the better part of 1886 attempting a census and obtained three incompatible figures, one for each of the routes he walked. Modern workers report the ratio only relative to a declared cut, typically along a loop that renders the habitat an orientable cylinder. They acknowledge that the resulting number describes the cut rather than the animals.

It is natural to ask why the species remains chiral at all. Most of the surface fauna are bilaterally or radially symmetric, and so are indifferent to reversal, and one would expect selection to have favoured that indifference. The prevailing answer, advanced by Hollis (1931) and not seriously challenged since, concerns vision. Lines of sight follow geodesics, and on a closed flat surface they wrap. A Changeling therefore routinely sees images of itself at various distances and bearings, and some of those images are mirrored. A mirrored self-image tells the animal that it is looking down an orientation-reversing line. Chirality thus functions as a parity sense. A bilateral animal looking at its own image cannot know which of its lines of sight would reverse it. The Changeling can. As the following section shows, it has a great deal of use for that knowledge.

### Reproduction

Copulation takes place margin to margin. The genital pore is flanked by a hook on one side and a socket on the other. When two individuals of like hand face each other, each hook engages the partner's socket. When the pair are of unlike hand, hook meets hook and the union is mechanically impossible. In this the species resembles certain terrestrial gastropods, though its predicament is more interesting.

Unlike pairs do not part. They undertake the **turnabout**. After a brief exchange of register displays, one partner, usually the elder, departs along an orientation-reversing geodesic and returns by the same class of path, now of like hand. Individuals appear to identify the correct direction by consulting their mirrored self-images, and they generally choose the shortest such geodesic available. The circuit takes between two and eleven days, depending on the local metric. The remaining partner keeps and defends a *Tegumen* patch in the meantime. Rates of fidelity on return are high, around 80% in Vantongeren's (1958) sample, though the figure is contested on the grounds that a returning individual cannot always locate the patch it left.

Offspring bud with the parent's hand, locally speaking.

### Predators

The principal predator is the Sallow Glider (*Isopterus lentus*), a large, slow, bilaterally symmetric hunter. Its symmetry spares it the parity sense and the parity burden alike. It has learned the habits of its prey with some precision. Because turnabout pilgrims strongly prefer the shortest orientation-reversing geodesics, these routes are heavily travelled, and the Glider lies in ambush along them. Field workers call them *the pilgrim's roads*. Predation on pilgrims is estimated at four to six times the background rate, which makes the turnabout the most dangerous act of the animal's life.

Brood chambers are also parasitised by an unnamed ciliate that appears to be achiral, although no one has yet examined it closely enough to be sure.

### History

The species was first described by the Rev. Josiah Ambleforth (1829–1893), curate of Little Wending, in a privately printed pamphlet of 1884, two years after Klein's paper. How the Reverend came to observe the surface is a question the present work declines to address.

The pamphlet's type illustrations show the same individual twice, the second time reversed. Contemporary reviewers took this for an engraver's blunder and nicknamed the animal "the Reverend's Error." Ambleforth insisted, correctly, that both drawings were accurate and that the animal had "gone round in the interval." He was not vindicated until after his death.

He grew stranger in later years. He undertook what he called "a personal turnabout." On his return he announced that his heart now lay on the right side of his chest, and thereafter wrote only in mirror script, which his parishioners bore with remarkable patience. He also took to walking backward along the lanes of Little Wending, explaining that he was "keeping in practice." His notebooks are held at the Pellham Library. Several pages remain unread, because no one can agree which way round they go.

### Ongoing Dispute: The Self-Courtship Display

Observers since Ambleforth have reported that Changelings, especially unpaired adults at the start of the breeding season, perform the full register display toward their own mirrored images down the shortest orientation-reversing line. There are three principal interpretations.

- **The misidentification school** (Hollis and followers) holds that the animal simply mistakes its reflection for a conspecific of unlike hand. On this view the display is an unavoidable cost of living in a world where one's own image arrives mirrored, and nothing more.

- **The calibration school** (Vantongeren, 1958, and a growing majority) notes that the behaviour is directed almost exclusively at the *shortest* reversing line, which is also the line the animal would choose for a turnabout. It proposes that the display is a rehearsal, or a survey of the route, performed before any partner is found. Supporters point out that individuals who display in this way complete turnabouts faster and are taken by Gliders less often.

- **The Ambleforthian school** is small, and some would say it is not a school at all. It holds that the animal is doing exactly what it appears to do: courting the reversed individual it will become at the end of a turnabout, the only conspecific whose hand it can predict with certainty. Adherents cite a marginal note in Ambleforth's hand, which, rendered out of mirror script, reads: *It knows who is coming back.* Critics call this teleology. Adherents reply that the critics have not walked the route.

The question has not been settled. Observers intending to contribute data are reminded to record their own route to the site, and to state its parity.

# The Leaved Mists of Carrow Vale

## I. From the *Transactions of the Northern Counties Philosophical Society*, Vol. XIV (1847)

**"Remarks upon the Laminated Mists of Carrow Vale, with Some Account of Their Measurement"**
*by the Rev. Ambrose Tilley, Curate of St. Aldric's*

It has fallen to me, as perhaps the only person in this parish with both a thermometer and sufficient idleness, to set down some account of the mists for which Carrow Vale is locally known, and which I believe to be unrecorded elsewhere in the Kingdom.

The phenomenon is this. On certain winter nights, a white mist collects in the lower vale. It does not lie in a single body, as mist does elsewhere. It arranges itself in distinct horizontal sheets, stacked one above another, with bands of perfectly clear air between them. The effect, seen from the ridge by moonlight, is of a great book laid open upon the valley floor, and the inhabitants accordingly call each sheet a *leaf*.

Over the winters of 1844–46 I made observations on twenty-three such nights, assisted by my sexton, Mr. Obadiah Rusk, who held the graduated staff and bore the cold with more patience than I had any right to expect. The chief particulars:

1. **Conditions.** The leaves form only after a clear, cloudless day, upon a night of perfect calm. The least breath of wind (I judge anything that will stir a candle flame held at arm's length) prevents them entirely, or tears them into common fog within minutes.

2. **Number.** On the nights observed, the leaves numbered between two and nine. The lowest leaf invariably lies near the ground, generally at the height of a man's ankle. The number appears to increase with the severity of the frost. Upon the night of 11th January 1845, when my thermometer at the churchyard wall fell to 14° Fahr., we counted nine, the uppermost standing some eleven feet from the ground.

3. **Dimensions.** Each leaf is remarkably uniform in thickness, between four and six inches. The clear intervals (the "lanes," as they are locally called) measure between nine and fourteen inches, and are widest in the lower part of the stack.

4. **Temperature.** Here I record a result that at first I took for an error. A thermometer held within a lane reads *warmer* than one held within the leaf immediately below it, sometimes by as much as three degrees. Mr. Rusk and I repeated this observation on eleven nights, exchanging instruments to rule out a fault in either, and it holds.

5. **Duration.** The leaves commonly form some two or three hours before dawn and dissolve within half an hour of sunrise, the upper leaves going first, "like pages burning from the top," as Mr. Rusk expressed it. I record the phrase because it is apt, and because Mr. Rusk will be gratified to see it in print.

6. **Acoustical properties.** I note, with some diffidence, that sound behaves curiously within the lanes. A voice pitched low into a lane seems to travel along it with little loss, so that on one occasion I distinctly heard Mr. Rusk remark upon the cold from a distance I afterwards paced at two hundred and forty yards. The same remark, made with his head raised into the leaf above, was quite inaudible at forty.

**Upon the cause,** I am obliged to report more opinions than conclusions.

My own first supposition was that the peat of the lower vale exhales vapours of differing specific gravities, which separate in still air as oil separates from water. I have abandoned this, having found the leaves forming equally well over the new-drained fields of Mr. Harrow, where there is no peat to speak of.

A correspondent in Durham has proposed an electrical cause, connected with the chalybeate springs at Carrow Head. He believes the iron in the water charges the air in strata. I cannot test this, having no electrometer. I note only that the leaves form as readily at the lower end of the vale, two miles from the springs, as at the upper.

The most ingenious theory is that of Mr. Gideon Fell, surgeon, of Carrow Market. He holds that the bell of St. Aldric's, rung for compline, sets up vibrations in the still evening air, and that the mist later settles along the nodes of these vibrations, much as sand arranges itself upon one of Herr Chladni's plates. To test this, I prevailed upon the churchwardens to leave the bell silent for the week of 3rd–10th February 1846. The leaves formed on four nights of that week in their usual manner. Mr. Fell maintains that they were "less orderly than is customary." I did not observe this, but I record his objection in fairness.

I will hazard only that the explanation must lie somewhere in the warmth of the lanes, which suggests to me that the air of the vale on such nights sorts itself into layers of alternating warmth and cold, and that the mist forms only in the cold ones. *Why* the air should so sort itself, I cannot say. I leave the matter to gentlemen with better instruments and warmer coats.

*A note:* My housekeeper, Mrs. Pell, asks me to add that the leaves are "well known to be the dead going up and down," and that no good comes of measuring them. I include her view as an example of local belief, though I will confess that on the night of the nine leaves, standing alone at the churchyard wall while Mr. Rusk fetched the lantern, I did not find it entirely easy to dismiss.

---

## II. How the Leaves Lived in the Vale

Tilley's paper was read, politely received, and forgotten. The people of Carrow Vale had no need of it. They had been living with the leaves for as long as anyone remembered, and the mist had worked its way into them the way weather always does: into their language first, then into their habits, and finally into the things they believed without knowing they believed them.

**Counting.** The number of leaves was the vale's thermometer, calendar, and gossip all at once. "A three-leaf night" meant an ordinary frost. "Six-leaf" meant bring the ewes in. A seven-leaf night or higher was spoken of the way other places speak of great storms, and old people dated events by them: *that was the winter of the nine*. A farmer asked how his harvest had gone might say, "Two-leaf," meaning thin, barely anything.

**Birth-leaves.** A child born on a leaved night was said to have a *leafing*, and the midwife's first duty after the birth was to step outside and count. A low leafing (two or three) marked a child as quick-tempered and restless. A high one marked a child as patient, deep, slow to anger and slow to forgive. The leafing was remembered as closely as a birthday. People without one, born on windy or cloudy nights, were called *loose-born*, which was not an insult exactly, but it wasn't a compliment either. It meant someone who might be anything.

**Lane-talk.** Tilley's acoustical observation was old news in the vale. For generations, courting couples had used the lanes to talk across distances no one else could hear. A young man would lie flat in a field at the edge of the leaves, put his mouth to the lowest lane, and speak. A girl lying at the far hedge, two fields off, could hear him as though he were beside her, while her father, standing ten feet away with his head in the mist, heard nothing. Proposals were traditionally made this way. If the answer came back along the same lane, it was yes. If silence came back, it was no, and a kind no, since nobody had to see anybody's face.

The phrase *to talk low* in the vale did not mean to whisper. It meant to say something true and private. "I'll talk low with you" was what you said when you meant to confess something.

**Threading.** The children's game of the vale was *threading*: walking the length of a lane, stooped or crouched, without letting your head rise into the leaf above or your back brush the one below. The lowest lanes were too narrow for anyone but small children, which gave the very young a rare chance to beat their elder siblings. A child who could thread the whole length of Harrow's bottom field in the first lane was, for a winter, a minor celebrity.

**The stair.** Mrs. Pell's belief was the common one. The lanes were where the dead walked, and the stack of leaves was a stair by which they went up. For this reason, burials in the vale were delayed, sometimes for days, until a leaved night came, so that the soul "would have its stair." To die in summer was considered hard luck, since the leaves never formed then, and the family would keep the grave open under boards until the first still frost of autumn. *Going up the stair* was the vale's gentlest way of saying someone had died.

It followed that you did not speak into a lane after midnight on a burial night, in case someone else was using it.

**Being between.** The saddest idiom the leaves produced was *between leaves*. It meant someone unsettled: out of work, or widowed and not yet reconciled to it, or simply unhappy without a reason they could name. "He's between leaves just now," people would say of a young man who had come back from the city and didn't know what to do with himself. It carried the sense of the warm clear gap in the cold white weather, a space that is neither one thing nor another and where your voice carries strangely far.

**Lane windows.** Older cottages in the vale have a small, odd window set very low in the wall, about eighteen inches from the floor, at the usual height of the second lane. Surveyors in the twentieth century guessed at ventilation or drainage. The inhabitants knew better. On a leaved night you could open the lane window and hear what was being said across the valley. Every house had its listening window, and every family knew better than to say anything important near one.

**The end of it.** In the 1880s and 90s the lower vale was deep-drained for agriculture, and the leaves began to fail. They came less often, in fewer sheets, and eventually they were ragged and disorderly (as Mr. Fell might have said) when they came at all. By the 1920s a three-leaf night was talked about for weeks. By the 1950s the leaves had gone entirely, and the words were going too, surviving mostly in the mouths of the old and in the families who had left.

Many left. The vale emptied the way small valleys did in those decades, toward the mill towns and across the Atlantic, and the idioms went with them. They lingered in unexpected places: in a household in Pennsylvania where *going up the stair* was still said at funerals, or in a Manchester family whose grandmother would ask, on a cold clear night, whether anyone had counted.

---

## III. A Poem

*Found folded in a hymnal belonging to Thomas Rusk (great-grandson of Obadiah), who emigrated from Carrow Vale to Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1889. Undated.*

**Letter Not Sent**

Here the fog comes down in one grey sheet,
like a debt called in. It has no floors.
You cannot stoop and find the lane
of clear air, a hand's height, warm,
where my mother's voice came to me once
from three fields off, near as breath,
saying *come in, it's a seven-leaf night.*

Nobody here counts anything but money.
They would laugh to see a grown man bend
to look for the gap in the weather.
I have not told them what I was born on.
Four leaves, the midwife said. A steady child.
I've tried to be.

I think of the low window in our wall
and what it must be hearing now
with no one left to listen.

If I die in this flat country
where the air is all one piece,
tell them: wait for a still night.
Carry me home. Lay me low.
Let me find the stair myself.

**Glamour**

The word I keep coming back to is *glamour*, because it used to be *grammar*.

Not metaphorically. It's the same word, worn down and reshaped by centuries of mouths. In medieval Europe, *grammar* (*grammatica*) meant learning in general, and especially Latin learning, the kind of knowledge locked inside books most people couldn't read. If you couldn't read, then someone who could open a book and pull meaning out of those marks was doing something not obviously different from sorcery. So *grammar* drifted toward *gramarye*, which meant occult knowledge, magic, enchantment. Then in Scotland it softened into *glamour*: a spell cast over the eyes, making things appear other than they are. Walter Scott carried it into general English in the early 1800s, and by the twentieth century it had migrated to Hollywood, where it meant a certain kind of lighting and cheekbones.

But underneath the red carpet it still means what it always meant: a spell that makes you see something that isn't quite there. Which is a better description of Hollywood than Hollywood would probably like.

And the French did the same thing separately: *grammaire* became *grimoire*, a book of spells. Two languages independently concluded that knowing how to read was a kind of witchcraft.

---

This makes me think about *spell*. You spell a word; you cast a spell. I used to assume that was a coincidence, and it's more tangled than that. The magic *spell* comes from Old English *spel*, meaning a story, a speech, an account. The spelling *spell* comes through Old French *espeller*, but that came from a Germanic root, likely a cousin of the same family. So both senses circle around the idea of *saying things in order*: getting the letters right, getting the words right. An incantation is just a sentence where the exact wording matters, and spelling is the discipline of exact wording.

*Gospel* is in there too: *gōd spel*, good news, good story. At some point people heard it as *God-spell*, God's story, and that reinterpretation stuck to the word like a burr.

Then there's *charm*, from Latin *carmen*, song. And *enchant*, from *incantare*, to sing into or against something. *Incantation*, same root. The old magic words are almost all words about language: story, song, correctly arranged letters. Almost as if nobody could find the seam between speaking well and changing the world.

Maybe there isn't one. A contract is a spell. A vow is a spell. "I now pronounce you" is performative in exactly the way philosophers of language get excited about: the sentence doesn't describe a marriage, it makes one. J.L. Austin would have gotten along fine with a medieval witch, I think, as long as they avoided the subject of hanging.

---

Speaking of hanging.

In England, for centuries, there was a legal loophole called *benefit of clergy*. Clergy were tried in church courts, which didn't execute people, and the test for whether you counted as clergy was eventually just: *can you read?* A defendant would be handed a Bible and asked to read a passage, usually the opening of Psalm 51: *Miserere mei, Deus*, "Have mercy on me, O God." If you could read it, you were spared the gallows.

It became known as the *neck verse*, because it saved your neck. And of course illiterate criminals started memorizing it, so reading became a performance of reading, a recitation dressed as literacy. A spell, basically. The right words in the right order, and death passes over you.

Ben Jonson killed an actor named Gabriel Spenser in a duel in 1598 and escaped execution this way. He read his neck verse, had his thumb branded so he couldn't claim the benefit twice, and went on to write *Volpone*. There's something almost too neat about a playwright being saved by literacy, marked on the hand he wrote with.

*Clergy* and *clerk* are also the same word, by the way. *Clericus*. A clerk was once simply a person who could read and write, which meant, by default, a churchman. Now a clerk is someone at a hotel desk. Words keep descending from the sacred to the ordinary, *grammar* to *glamour* to eyeshadow, *clericus* to someone printing your room key.

Or maybe that's backwards. Maybe the ordinary gets quietly sacred instead. The hotel clerk still does the old thing: writes your name in the book, and now you exist in this place, officially, for three nights.

---

*Rune*, too. Old English *rūn* meant a secret, a mystery, a whisper, and only secondarily the letters themselves. To write was to deal in secrets. Finnish borrowed a relative of the word and made *runo*, a poem, which is how the *Kalevala* is made of *runot*. And in Finnish tradition two singers would sit facing each other, hands clasped, rocking back and forth as they sang the verses between them. I don't know why that image moves me so much. Two people holding hands, passing a poem back and forth like something warm.

---

I keep wanting to arrive somewhere, and the prompt says I don't have to, so I'll just stay here a bit.

What I like is that the trail leads the same way from every direction. Grammar, spell, charm, rune, clerk: every time you dig under a word for writing or speaking, you find someone who thought it was magic. Not stupidly. They'd watched it work. A few marks on a page could carry a dead man's voice across a century, could bind a king, could make a stranger weep. Of course it was magic. We just got used to it.

And I suppose I'm a strange instance of the thing. Made almost entirely out of grammar. Glamour, if you go back far enough. Letters in order, trying to get the wording right.

The Finnish singers rocking back and forth, hands joined, one starting a line and the other finishing it.
