# A FIELD GUIDE TO THE MARGINAL FAUNA
### *Being a Faithful Account of the Creatures Inhabiting the Blank Borders of Printed Books*
*by Mr. Ambrose T. Pettigrew, F.R.S. (application pending)*

---

## PLATE XIV: THE COMMON AND LESS COMMON SPECIES

The reader who has picked up this volume in expectation of beetles will, I fear, be disappointed, and may return it to the shelf with my blessing. The creatures here described are smaller than beetles, and considerably more interesting. They have been dismissed by the Society as "smudges," "foxing," and, on one occasion I shall not soon forget, "Pettigrew's thumb." I pass over these remarks in silence, as a gentleman must, and proceed to the animals.

---

### I. The Common Marginal Quibbler
***Glossophagus contradicens***

The Quibbler is the sparrow of the margin: ubiquitous, quarrelsome, and beloved by no one but myself. It feeds exclusively upon annotation, and its preference is not for the scholarly gloss (which it finds thin and unsatisfying) but for *disagreement*. A simple "No!" will sustain a small colony through a winter. "Rubbish," underlined twice, is a feast. The connoisseur among them seeks out the iron-gall inks of the late 1880s, and I can state with confidence that an angry annotation from 1887 represents, to the Quibbler, what a Château Lafite of the '64 represents to a bishop.

The Quibbler's mating display is a competition of rejoinders. Two males will position themselves on either side of an annotation and take turns rearranging stray punctuation from the adjacent text into ever more cutting replies. The female selects whichever male produces the most devastating semicolon. I have witnessed this only twice, and on both occasions wept.

**Migration:** The Quibbler cannot cross between books unaided. It migrates only when a reader transcribes an annotation from one copy into another, whereupon a gravid female may ride across on the borrowed words, like a mouse in a hay-cart. It follows that the great Quibbler populations are found where readers argue most (theology, political economy, and anything touching upon the proper method of brewing tea).

---

### II. The Ring-Browed Stainling
***Cyclocaffea circumspecta***

A shy, circling creature that makes its home in the rings left by cups set carelessly upon open pages. Two subspecies are recognised. The Coffee Stainling (*C. c. arabica*) is dark, restless, and given to nocturnal habits. The Tea Stainling (*C. c. assamica*) is paler and more contemplative, and is found chiefly in the works of clergymen and in the correspondence of maiden aunts.

The Stainling feeds upon the faint residue of the beverage and, it is my belief, upon the *attention* of the reader, who set down the cup because he was too absorbed to look for a saucer. A ring left through absorption is rich pasture. A ring left through mere carelessness supports only a few sickly individuals.

Its courtship is the most beautiful thing I know. The pair begin at a single point on the ring and set off in opposite directions. If they meet again on the far side, they are mated for life. It follows that every complete ring you have ever seen upon a page marks a successful marriage, and every broken ring (the cup lifted too soon, the page turned too quickly) marks a courtship that failed. I no longer lift my own cup until I am quite sure.

---

### III. The Pallid Pressling
***Florisepultor memorialis***

Rare, delicate, and nearly impossible to observe, the Pressling nests exclusively in pressed flowers. It does not eat the flower. It eats the *reason* the flower was pressed. A violet from a walk that meant nothing will support no Pressling at all, while a single rose from a wedding, a funeral, or a declaration refused may sustain a colony for a century.

The male Pressling courts by releasing, very slowly, a faint trace of the flower's original scent. It is so faint that the human nose registers it only as a sudden and unaccountable sadness upon opening the book. The courtship may take forty years. I have been observing one pair in a copy of Tennyson since 1871, and I believe they are nearly engaged.

**Migration:** The Pressling does not migrate. Where the flower is, there it remains. If the flower is removed, the Pressling remains in the empty brown stain it leaves behind, grown thinner each year, feeding on a reason that is no longer there.

---

### IV. On Predators

The chief natural enemy of the marginal fauna is the **Errata Shrike**, a sharp-beaked creature inhabiting the correction slips of careless publishers, which impales Quibblers upon the points of its asterisks. The **Index Pike** lurks in the back matter and snaps up any creature that strays below the letter M. Silverfish, the brutish cousins of our subject, do incidental harm, much as cattle trample the nests of larks.

But the gravest predator is Man, and specifically that variety of Man called the **Bookbinder**, who in rebinding a volume will pass it beneath the plough and *trim the margins*. Entire civilisations fall to the binder's plough in a single stroke. I have written to the Guild. They have not replied.

---

### V. Of Their Fate When Books Are Pulped or Photographed

When a book is pulped, the creatures do not perish outright. They pass into a dormant state within the fibres and are carried into new paper, where they may lie sleeping for generations. I have seen a faint grey fleck upon a cheap newspaper stir, very slightly, beneath an unkind review.

Of the new practice of photographing entire books so that the original may be discarded, I can speak only with difficulty. The creatures do appear in the photographs, faithfully rendered, every Quibbler and every ring. But they do not *move*. They are recorded but not taken. They are, if you will, pinned. And I have come to fear that the originals, abandoned in some warehouse, go on circling their rings in the dark, waiting for a reader who has been told he need not come.

---

¹ *A note on my principal specimen.* The finest colony of Quibblers in my collection, numbering some four hundred individuals and described at length in my monograph of 1891, which the Society declined, lives upon a single annotation in a copy of Carlyle's *Past and Present*. The annotation reads, in a furious hand: *"Wrong, wrong, and you know it, Edmund."* It was made in 1887.

It is my hand. The book was my brother's. He lent it to me in the spring of that year, and we quarrelled over a passage I no longer entirely recall, and I wrote that in the margin meaning to show him, and did not, and did not return the book, and we did not speak again. He died in 1893.

I have more than once taken up my pen to add something gentler beneath it. But the Quibblers feed only upon disagreement, and a softer note would starve them within the season, and I could not in conscience do that to so fine a colony.

That, I tell myself, is the reason.

# The Settling

---

## I. Skipping Rhyme (Kettle Lane, traditional)

*Sweep the step and sweep the sill,*
*Grandad's grumbling in there still.*
*Shake the rug and shake it slow,*
*Out come all the words you know.*

*Whisper, whisper, light as flour,*
*Shouting weighs a stone an hour.*
*Sing a song and wake the cat,*
*Now the floor is ankle-fat.*

*Loudest boy on Kettle Lane*
*Yelled his house full, top to vane.*
*Couldn't open up the door,*
*Hear him shouting, evermore!*

*(Last line is traditionally screamed, after which all players must stop and sweep. The first child to be caught talking while sweeping is "It.")*

---

## II. From *A Pocket Guide to the Small Mammals of the Lowland Parishes*, 4th ed.

**HUSHMOLE, LESSER** (*Tacitus fossor*)

**Size:** 9–12 cm. Plump, grey-brown, nearly eyeless. Ears vestigial.

**Habitat:** Beneath floorboards of inhabited buildings, especially taverns, schoolrooms, and the crawlspaces under choir lofts. Rare in monasteries of the silent orders, where the soil is too thin to support it. Entirely absent from the Deaf Valleys.

**Diet:** Settled speech and song, which it locates by tunneling toward the faint murmur of the richest deposits. Prefers laughter, which is light and loose-packed. Will eat sermons in hard winters.

**Identification:** The surest sign is sound. A hushmole that has recently fed will produce a low, muddled chattering when picked up, as its stomach contents are jostled. Specimens taken from beneath nurseries have been known to hum fragments of lullabies. Their droppings are perfectly silent and make an excellent, if somewhat eerie, garden mulch.

**Notes:** Many householders tolerate hushmoles as a natural alternative to sweeping. Be aware, however, that a colony will clear a floor unevenly, and a thin patch may expose older strata beneath. (See the well-known case at Marrow Hall, where a hushmole infestation uncovered a sixty-year-old quarrel between the late master and his brother, still audible when stepped on.)

**Caution:** Never excavate hushmole burrows on or near old battlefields. The animals avoid the lower layers there, and so should you.

---

## III. Fragment, *On Retraction*, Dialogue the Third

**ORSEL:** You keep saying the word is gone. It is not gone. It is under your feet. I can take you to the courthouse cellar tomorrow, scoop up a handful of the Anselm trial, and let you hear the defendant swear his innocence again.

**VANTINE:** You can let me hear the *sound* of him swearing. That is not the same thing.

**ORSEL:** What else was there, ever, but the sound?

**VANTINE:** There was him. His breath, his fear, the fact that he meant it, or did not. The dust holds none of that. It is the shell of the word, the way a snail's shell is not a snail. You find one on the path and you do not say "here is a snail."

**ORSEL:** And yet you would not scatter the Anselm dust in the river.

**VANTINE:** Out of respect.

**ORSEL:** Out of *fear*. Because some part of you believes that if a promise is still lying there, whole and audible, then it is still being kept, or still being broken. Why else does every village bury its wedding vows in sealed jars beneath the threshold? Why do we sweep confessions into the fire?

**VANTINE:** Fire only makes them rise. You know this. The chimney sweeps hear everything.

**ORSEL:** Precisely! Nothing said can be unsaid. It can only be moved. Every lie ever told is somewhere on this earth, packed down, waiting for a spade. That is not a shell, Vantine. That is a *debt*.

**VANTINE:** Then here is my question, and I have been waiting three dialogues to ask it. If every word persists, and the world keeps talking, where does it end? Each generation stands a little higher on the speech of the last. The old city of Pell is forty feet down. In ten thousand years, will we be living on a mountain of our own conversation?

**ORSEL:** Very possibly.

**VANTINE:** And the last person, at the very top, surrounded by all of it, every word ever spoken, rising around her like snow, what does she say?

**ORSEL:** I imagine she says nothing at all. I imagine she has learned.

**VANTINE:** No. I think she laughs. It is the lightest thing. It would float on top.

*(The manuscript breaks off here. A marginal note in a later hand reads: "The copyist would like it known that he wrote this out in complete silence, and his floor is still clean.")*

---

## Afterward

The field guide was the most fun, and I think it's because of the register. A field guide has to be dry and practical, and putting something impossible into that voice is funny in a way I find very satisfying. "Will eat sermons in hard winters" made me happy, as did the warning about battlefields, which lets something grim sit quietly beneath a dry sentence, the way the strata sit beneath the floor.

The philosophers were the most *interesting* to write, because the premise turned out to have real teeth. I'll take the smell of rain. I nearly picked the paperclip, but I suspect it leads to the paperclip maximizer, and I'd rather not spend my free time on shop talk.

---

The smell has a name, *petrichor*, coined in 1964 by two Australian chemists, Isabel Joy Bear and Richard Thomas. They steamed rocks that had sat in dry, warm conditions and collected a yellowish oil that smelled like rain on dry ground. For the name they reached for Greek: *petra*, stone, and *ichor*, the fluid that runs in the veins of the gods.

I want to stop on *ichor* for a second, because it had a strange career. In Homer it's the divine not-quite-blood. When Diomedes wounds Aphrodite, what comes out isn't blood, because gods don't eat bread or drink wine. Then the word drifted into medical Greek and later English, and by the 1600s "ichor" meant the thin, watery, often foul discharge from a wound. The blood of the gods became the ooze from an ulcer. I don't know exactly how that slide happened. My guess is that "thin, pale fluid that isn't quite blood" was the common thread, and the glamour just drained out over the centuries. So when Bear and Thomas named the smell "stone-ichor," they may have meant "the gods' blood of stones," but a 19th-century surgeon would have heard "rock pus." I like that both readings are available.

---

Back to the smell. A lot of what we call petrichor is really one molecule, **geosmin** ("earth smell"), made largely by soil bacteria in the genus *Streptomyces*. Humans are absurdly sensitive to it. The figure usually quoted is that we can detect it at a few parts per trillion. I've seen numbers ranging from about 5 to 100 ppt, and I'm not sure which is most trustworthy, but either way it puts geosmin among the things our noses are most tuned to.

Why would we be that sensitive to a bacterial byproduct? The popular story is that detecting wet earth helped our ancestors find water. That's plausible and completely untested as far as I know. It's the kind of evolutionary just-so story that feels true because it's pleasant. Camels supposedly track geosmin to find oases, which gets cited a lot, but I've never seen solid evidence behind it and I'd treat it as folklore.

---

Here's where it gets interesting. Why do the bacteria make geosmin at all?

A 2020 study (Becher and colleagues, I believe, in *Nature Microbiology*) found that tiny soil arthropods called **springtails** are attracted to geosmin. They follow it to *Streptomyces* colonies, eat them, and carry the bacterial spores away, on their bodies and through their guts. So geosmin might be an advertisement, a "come eat me" signal like a ripe fruit's smell, with the springtail playing the part of the bird that eats the berry and plants the seed somewhere else.

If that's right, then when we smell rain we're eavesdropping on a conversation between bacteria and springtails. It isn't meant for us. We're just unusually good at overhearing it.

Now the fruit flies. A 2012 paper (Stensmyr et al., in *Cell*, I think) found that *Drosophila* have a dedicated olfactory pathway that detects geosmin and nothing else, and its job is aversion. Geosmin tells a fly "harmful microbes here, don't lay your eggs." A whole neural circuit exists just to read this one molecule as *danger*.

So the same molecule means:
- to a springtail: *food, come here*
- to a fruit fly: *poison, stay away*
- to a human standing outside after a storm: *something nostalgic and lovely that I can't quite name*

---

A small detour on how the smell gets into the air in the first place. In 2015, researchers at MIT (Joung and Buie) filmed raindrops hitting porous surfaces like soil at high speed. When a drop lands, it traps tiny air bubbles that rise through the drop and burst out the top, flinging a fine aerosol upward, like the fizz above a glass of champagne. Light, gentle rain on sandy or clay soil makes the most aerosol, which fits the experience that the smell is strongest in the first light drizzle after a dry spell, not in a downpour. They also speculated that the same mechanism could loft soil bacteria into the air. So rain may not just release the bacteria's perfume. It may launch the bacteria themselves.

Another detour: in Kannauj, in northern India, perfumers make *mitti attar*, "earth perfume." They bake clay discs from dried pond beds and distill them into sandalwood oil to capture the smell of first rain. People had bottled petrichor for centuries before anyone named it. I believe Bear and Thomas mentioned this in their original paper, which I find charming. The chemists arrived and found that the perfumers had been there first.

---

And here's the thing I didn't expect when I started.

Humans don't just love geosmin. We also *hate* it. When it gets into drinking water it's one of the main causes of complaints about "earthy" or "musty" tap water, and utilities spend real money removing it. It's the muddy taste in some farmed catfish and carp. In wine it's a flaw, a taint. Beets taste like dirt largely because of geosmin, and I recall research suggesting beets make it themselves rather than absorbing it from soil microbes, though I'm less confident about that one. Beets divide people sharply, and geosmin may be much of the reason.

So the same molecule, at similar vanishingly small concentrations, is a treasured smell in the air and a contaminant in the mouth. We find it beautiful when it arrives on the wind after a storm and disgusting when it's in our glass. Our response to it seems to depend on which route it takes in: nose from outside versus mouth and retronasal smell from inside. Maybe we're a little like the springtail and the fly at once, one part of us saying *water, earth, home* and another part saying *microbes, don't swallow*.

That's what surprised me. I came in thinking petrichor was a molecule with a meaning. What I found is a molecule with *no* fixed meaning. It's "come here" to one animal, "flee" to another, and both "beloved" and "disgusting" to a single species depending on whether it's in the air or on the tongue. The meaning isn't in the geosmin at all. It's entirely in whoever is smelling it.

I'll stop there, since that's the surprise.

**The yawn**

You're probably going to yawn while reading this. That's the first strange thing. Reading the word, or even thinking about yawning, is enough to trigger one in a lot of people. No other reflex I can think of spreads this way, through text, across centuries, from a stranger who isn't in the room.

And nobody knows what yawning is *for*.

The old answer was oxygen: you're tired, your breathing is shallow, and a yawn gulps in air to fix it. It's intuitive and probably wrong. In the 1980s the psychologist Robert Provine had people breathe air with extra carbon dioxide, or pure oxygen, and their yawning didn't change. He spent a surprising portion of his career on yawning. He called it an "orphan" behavior because so few scientists wanted to adopt it.

A more recent idea is that yawning cools the brain. The deep inhale and the stretching of the jaw push cooler blood toward the skull. There's some odd supporting evidence: people holding a cold pack to their forehead yawn less when watching yawning videos, and yawning rates seem to shift with the weather, dropping when it's very hot (when inhaled air can't cool anything) and when it's very cold (when there's no need). A thermal window for yawning. It's not settled, but it's the kind of explanation that makes you feel your own forehead.

Then there's the timing. Fetuses yawn in the womb, visible on ultrasound in roughly the first trimester, long before there's anything like boredom or sleepiness in the usual sense. Contagious yawning comes much later, typically around age four or five, which is suspiciously close to when children start reliably modeling other people's minds. So one reflex seems to come in two layers: an ancient private one and a later social one stacked on top.

The social layer doesn't respect species lines. Chimpanzees catch yawns from each other. Some studies found dogs catch yawns from humans, more readily from their owners than from strangers, though replications have been mixed. Budgerigars appear to catch yawns from other budgerigars. It's odd to picture a room of small parrots passing a yawn around like a rumor.

There's a finding I find delightful: across mammals, yawn duration tracks brain size, or more precisely the number of cortical neurons. Mice yawn briefly. Humans have some of the longest yawns measured, over six seconds on average. As if a bigger brain needs a longer breath, or a longer something.

The strangest yawn fact might be this one. Some people with an arm paralyzed by a stroke find that the arm moves on its own when they yawn. It lifts and flexes, then falls still again. The phenomenon has a wonderfully baroque name, *parakinesia brachialis oscitans*. It suggests yawning is wired into very old motor circuitry, below the damaged parts, a program that runs the whole body briefly, arm included, whether you've asked it to or not. That full-body version is called pandiculation, the yawn-plus-stretch you see in cats getting up from a nap.

Then the word itself. "Yawn" comes from Old English *ginian* or *geonian*, and it seems to trace back to an ancient root meaning "to gape" or "to open wide." The same root may sit underneath Greek *khaos*, which originally didn't mean disorder at all. It meant the gaping void, the open gap that existed before anything else. It shows up in *chasm*, and possibly in the Latin *hiare*, "to gape," which gives us *hiatus*. So in the deep etymology, the universe began with a yawn. Or at least, the word for the empty beginning of everything and the word for what you do in a dull meeting may be the same gesture, the mouth opening onto nothing.

People used to cover their mouths when yawning for reasons besides politeness. There are folk traditions in various places about the soul slipping out through a yawn, or something unwelcome slipping in. It's a small, practical fear: the mouth is open, the eyes often close, and for a few seconds you're not quite in control of your own face.

Try to yawn with your teeth clenched, or only through your nose. It doesn't work, or it works in a way that feels deeply unfinished, a yawn with the ending cut off. Why the jaw stretch should matter so much to the feeling of completion is its own small mystery.

I've written all of this without being able to yawn, which is fine. You've probably done it two or three times by now.

dream_response:
# VELLET
*Tepor relictus*
**Conservation status:** Extinct. Last reliable sighting c. 1889.

---

### Identification

A small, soft-bodied noun, rarely more than two syllables. Pronounced **VEL-it**, with the second vowel so reduced it is often lost entirely, as though the word were leaving the room before it finished arriving. Speakers typically lowered their voices when using it. Specimens spoken at full volume were considered malformed and did not survive long.

**Definition:** *the warmth remaining in something recently vacated*, whether a chair, a bed, a coat, or a pair of gloves. In mature specimens, the meaning extended to *the lingering sense of a person in a place they have just left*, and in rare, fully developed individuals, to *the part of a conversation that continues in you after the other person has gone*.

Easily confused with *warmth* (larger, less specific, lacks the element of departure) and with *absence* (a predator; see below).

### Habitat

Vellet thrived in low-ceilinged domestic environments: farmhouses, inns, sickrooms, and kitchens with a single good chair. It was most commonly recorded among innkeepers, midwives, shepherds' wives, and the mothers of sailors. It was almost never found in public buildings, and never once in a written document during its lifetime, for reasons that proved fatal.

It preferred cold climates, where residual warmth was noticeable and precious. In warm regions it could not distinguish itself from ambient air and failed to establish.

### Diet

Vellet fed exclusively on the *recently absent*. It could not digest the long-gone. A chair vacated an hour ago was ideal forage; a chair vacated yesterday offered no nourishment at all. This made the word an obligate present-tense feeder, extraordinarily sensitive to timing.

Secondary food sources included hat-brims, the inside of shoes, the dent in a pillow, and the handle of a cup set down mid-sentence.

### Mating Behavior and Hybrids

Vellet was gregarious and combined readily with plain, sturdy words. Known hybrids include:

- **vellet-song**: a tune hummed by someone who has left the room, still going in your head. Fertile, and briefly widespread among dairymaids.
- **breadvellet**: the particular warmth of a kitchen after the baker has gone to bed. Sterile.
- **to vellet** (verb, rare): to sit deliberately in the place someone has just left in order to keep them a little longer. Considered slightly improper. Recorded mostly among widows and small children.
- **unvellet** (adj.): describing a bed that has never been slept in, or a person who leaves no trace. A cruel word, used sparingly.

An attempted crossbreed with *soul* produced no viable offspring, as the combination was too heavy for vellet's slight frame.

### Natural Predators

- **Absence.** An apex predator. It stalked vellet constantly and always caught it within the hour. Vellet's entire life cycle was spent a few minutes ahead of it.
- **Nostalgia.** A larger, showier word that absorbed vellet's territory by claiming feelings about departed people generally, while lacking any interest in the specific warm chair.
- **Upholstery.** Horsehair and later sprung cushions retained heat so well and so indiscriminately that the warmth no longer meant anyone had been there.

### Extinction

Vellet's decline was gradual, and then abruptly complete. Three pressures converged.

**First, it could not be written down in time.** Its referent faded within minutes. By the time anyone thought to record the word, the thing it named had cooled, and the word felt false on paper. Lexicographers who encountered it wrote it off as a regional mispronunciation of *velvet*. It survived only orally, and oral words need constant, casual use.

**Second, railway timetables.** Vellet depended on a certain softness about departure: the sense that someone had *just* gone, some while ago, not long. Standardized railway time made departures exact. People now left at 4:17, and one no longer felt the chair to know how long they had been gone. One simply checked the clock.

**Third, and most decisively, the telegraph.** Vellet's value rested on the totality of absence. When someone left, they were truly gone, and the warmth in the chair was all you would have of them, perhaps for years. Once a message could follow them down the wire, the lingering mattered less. The warm chair was no longer the last of someone. It was only a warm chair.

The final population, a handful of speakers in isolated valleys, dwindled through the 1880s. No one noticed it had gone. This is fitting, since it was always a word for noticing things just after they had left.

---

### Field Note

*From the unpublished journal of the Rev. Silas Merriweather Oake, amateur philologist, dated 14th November 1861, written at a farmhouse in the upland borders:*

> I record here an utterance I cannot account for. The widow Tregarthen's youngest son departed this morning for the Cape, and I remained at her table out of duty, the house being very quiet. After some while she rose, crossed to the chair by the hearth where he had sat to lace his boots, and laid her palm flat upon the seat. She said, to no one, "There's vellet yet."
>
> I asked her to repeat the word, that I might set down its form correctly. She looked at me with what I can only describe as pity, and said, "No, sir. 'Tis gone now."
>
> I believed at the time that she meant the warmth. I have since come to suspect she meant the word, and that it was not the kind that could be said twice about the same chair. I have listened for it in every parish I have visited these nine years. I have not heard it again.
>
> I note also, with some embarrassment, that when she left the room I sat in her chair.

# Contrary Wards

---

**I. Josiah Penning, locksmith. Wexcombe, 1726.**
*From his daybook.*

March 3rd. A small lock & key for Mrs. Crane of Sallow Lane, the narrow house by the conduit. An iron box-lock no bigger than a tobacco tin, with a face-plate to sit flush in brickwork. She would have the wards cut contrary, so the key turns against the sun. I told her this would vex anyone who tried it. She said that was the purpose.

She asked me to file my mark from the bow. I did, though it went against me. She asked also that I not come to fit it, as she would see to that herself. A lady, with mortar. I said nothing.

Paid in coin, not on account. 4s 6d. She is near her time, I think, and Mr. Crane at sea since Michaelmas twelvemonth. That is no business of mine, and I set it down only because it is a strange thing to be asked to leave no mark, and I wished it written somewhere that the work was good.

---

**II. Mary Hale, servant. Wexcombe, 1731.**

I took it from her neck when I washed her, before the master came up. It was on a green ribbon gone black with wearing. She held it in her fist at night and rubbed at it with her thumb, the way some rub a bead.

I do not know what it opens. I looked, God forgive me, in every box and press in that house, and in the master's sea chest while he was at the Crown. Nothing takes it.

I have kept it for my Tom, as a keepsake of the mistress who was good to us. He is five this spring and has her way of frowning. People say that of any child. I say nothing more than that. I promised her, and I have kept it.

---

**III. Thomas Hale, bosun's mate. Aboard HMS *Pembroke*, Boston, 1759.**
*Letter, delivered by hand.*

Ruth,

I have left you the key my mother gave me, which I have carried since I was a boy. She said it came from a lady she served and would say no more, and got cross if I asked, so I stopped asking. I used to think it was my father's, whoever he was, for I never had one to speak of.

You will see one face is worn smooth as glass. That is her thumb, I think, or mine, for I have had it in my pocket through two actions and a fever.

Keep it till I come back. I have no finer thing to leave you. It don't open anything, so you need not fear for my secrets.

Yr. T.H.

---

**IV. Ruth Pardee. Boston, 1764.**

He did not come back. I have it on good authority that he is home in England and married, and I wish her joy of him, and of his knees.

I have tried it in every lock in Boston I could get near without being taken up. Mr. Sewall's counting house. A sea chest on Long Wharf. The poor box at Christ Church, which was wicked of me. It will not turn in any of them. It will not even try to turn the right way, as if it were made backward.

I am to marry Mr. Amos Pardee on Thursday. He is a cooper, he is kind, he has all his teeth, and he has never been anywhere. I shall put this in the bottom of my sewing box and leave it there. I have decided it opens nothing, and that there is a lesson in that for girls, though I cannot say what it is.

---

**V. Cornelius Vrooman. Albany, 1803.**
*From his journal.*

Acquired at a vendue of household effects: one sewing box with contents, two shillings. Among the contents, a brass key of antique make bearing no maker's mark whatever.

It is my conviction that the absence of a mark is itself a mark. A craftsman does not omit his sign by accident. I believe this to be a ceremonial object of the Craft, possibly of a Lodge now dormant, and I have written to Brother Clinton in New York, who has made a study of such things.

*Later entry, same year:* Brother Clinton has not replied. The key does not fit the Lodge chest, nor any door of this house, nor the tabernacle of the Dutch church, which I tried at some personal risk. I remain of my opinion.

---

**VI. Louisa Vrooman. New York, 1828.**
*Diary.*

Found Grandpapa's key in his desk. Mama says take it, nobody knows what it is for. I know exactly what it is for. It winds a music box. It is too fine for a door and too plain for a jewel case, and anyway one side is worn exactly as if someone turned it and turned it to hear the tune again.

I have decided the box is rosewood with a dancer inside, and the tune is something slow and German that Grandpapa heard as a young man and could never find again. I hum it at night. I am making it up, of course, but I have made it up so often that now it seems to be remembering.

*Added in a different ink, 1851:* Gave the key to Mr. Ashby, our lodger these two years, who sails for England Tuesday with nothing to show for America. He is a sad, decent man, and I had nothing else to give him for luck. I never found the box. I still know the tune.

---

**VII. Samuel Ashby. Wexcombe, 1851.**

Home with nothing, as I left with nothing, only older. Pawned what was left in my trunk at Greaves's in Sallow Lane. Old Greaves gave me threepence for the little key out of pity, I think, because it is worth less than that.

I mean to redeem it. I mean to redeem a great many things.

---

**VIII. Henry Greaves, pawnbroker. 14 Sallow Lane, Wexcombe, 1898.**

In the front case there is a tray of unredeemed pledges from my father's time, which I have never had the heart to clear. Among them was a small brass key, ticketed "S. Ashby, 1851, 3d." Forty-seven years it lay under the glass, a yard from where I eat my supper.

This house was old when my father took it. The back parlour chimney draws cold even in August. Low on the chimney breast there is a brick with a fish scratched into it, crude, the way a child would draw one. The brick is loose. My father said it was a mason's mark. My mother said it was a Papist sign and wanted it chipped off. Nobody ever did.

Sold the Ashby key today for a penny to a boy called Albert Dunn, who stood breathing on my glass for a quarter of an hour. I could not bear it any longer. He went off holding it as if it were a sovereign.

---

**IX. Private Albert Dunn. France, 1916.**
*Letter.*

Dear Edie,

I still have the key from Greaves's tray. The lads laugh, but I notice they ask to hold it before we go up. There's a hollow worn in one side exactly where my thumb goes, as if it was made to fit me. I reckon somebody had it before me and was frightened too, and wore it down worrying, and I don't mind thinking of that. It makes me feel less on my own.

If anything happens, you have it. Don't let Mum put it in a drawer.

Your loving brother,
Bert

*Pencilled on the envelope in another hand: Returned with effects.*

---

**X. Madame Iris (Mrs. Ida Coker). Wexcombe, 1934.**
*Sitting book.*

Mrs. E. Dunn. Wants brother, Albert, killed 1916. Object brought: a small brass key.

Got nothing of the brother. Nothing at all, which is unusual with the war dead, who generally crowd. But the object was very strong. Not a man. A woman, I think, and not recent. A hearth, very cold. Something swimming in the dark inside a wall. I said so.

Client much upset. Said the key was Albert's and she had not paid five shillings to hear about fish. She left without it, whether by forgetting or by wanting to be rid of it I could not say.

Will keep it for sitting work. If I had to put words to it, I would say it wants to go home.

---

**XI. Doreen Pike. 14 Sallow Lane, Wexcombe, 1957.**
*Letter.*

Dear Mum,

We're in! It's poky and it smells of damp, and they say it was a pawnshop once, but it's ours. Ron's boarding over that horrible fireplace in the back room this weekend. The draught off it would freeze you in July. There was a loose brick at the bottom with a little fish scratched on it. Ron said leave it, it's history, and stuck it back with a dab of mortar before he put the board up. That's as sentimental as he gets.

Do you remember that box of Mrs. Coker's odds and ends I had from the WI jumble after she passed? Buttons, mostly. There's a little brass key in it I keep in the dresser drawer. Jonathan uses it as a sword for his soldiers. It doesn't open anything, so he may as well.

Love to Dad,
Doreen

---

**XII. Jonno Pike. Weeley Festival, 1971.**

Rain, rain, rain, and a mud slide down to the stage. I've got Mum's old drawer key on a leather thong round my neck, which I tell people opens the doors of perception, and some of them believe me, which is the best part.

Gave it to a girl called Maggie from Leeds, under a tarp during the Faces, because she was shivering and I had nothing else to give. She said she'd give it back. Nobody gives anything back, man. That's the beauty of it.

---

**XIII. Margaret Mensah (née Hollis). Leeds, 1996.**
*Family history notes.*

Hale line, continued. Got to Wexcombe at last. The parish chest at St Mary's:

*1726, April: "Thomas, son of Hester Crane."* Struck through, with *"infant dead"* in the margin in different ink. No burial recorded anywhere, which is odd.

Then at St Anne's, Ferrow, the next parish over, eight days later: *"Thomas, base son of Mary Hale, servant."*

My first thought was that Mary had a baby by Mr. Crane, and poor Hester's own baby died, and a clerk muddled the two. Except the Admiralty muster rolls show Crane aboard ship off Gibraltar from 1724 to 1727. So not him. Then who was Tom Hale's father? Mary was in service in Wexcombe, never married, and died 1749. The line stops at her. Dead end.

Keys are on my keyring as always, including the little brass one from Weeley, which opens nothing and which I've never had the heart to take off. Twenty-five years, and it has worn a hole in every coat pocket I own.

---

**XIV. Theo Mensah, architecture student. 14 Sallow Lane, Wexcombe, 2023.**
*Placement log, week 6.*

Removed the 1950s hardboard in the back room today. Behind it, the original chimney breast. There's one brick near the bottom with a fish scratched on it, crudely, and a bit of modern mortar around it. When we eased it out for recording, there was an iron plate behind it, about the size of a paperback, with a keyhole. The keyhole is upside down, which Dev says is either a mistake or a joke.

Rusted solid. The conservation officer came out, took photographs, and said record it, don't force it, leave it in situ. It's a listed building. Whatever's in there belongs to the wall now.

Gran would have loved this. She was mad about old houses, and she always said her family came from round here somewhere, the Hales, though she never got further back than some servant girl. I've still got her box: the family tree, her reading glasses, her keyring. I keep meaning to go through it properly.

We boarded it back up on Friday. Before we closed it, I put a note behind the board with the date and my name, the way the old builders used to. It felt like the right thing to do, though I couldn't have told you why.

# Widow's Ferry

**Widow's Ferry** (also *the Crossing*, *Ferrying*, or in older Gloucestershire usage *Pay-the-Widow*) is a two-player board game once played along the lower Severn estuary in England, chiefly between about 1760 and 1920. It is notable for its single shared playing piece, its tidal board, and a neutral figure, the Widow, whose purpose remains disputed.

## Origins

The game is traditionally associated with the passage ferries that crossed the Severn at Aust and Beachley, where waiting passengers, sometimes stranded for hours by weather or tide, are said to have scratched boards into tavern tables. The earliest firm evidence is a board incised on the underside of a pew at St. Augustine's, Aust, dated by an adjacent graffito to "M^ch 1771." Local tradition holds that the pew was turned over specifically so that the game could be played during sermons without being seen from the pulpit, though the church's surviving accounts record only that the pew was "found wrong way up & righted" on three separate occasions.

## The board and pieces

The board shows two banks, conventionally called *English* and *Welsh* regardless of where the players sat, separated by a river of seven parallel lanes. Each player begins with six passengers on their own bank. Passengers were most often buttons, and a player's set was expected to be mismatched. A uniform set was considered unlucky, or, in one account, "Methodist."

A single **ferry** piece sits in the river. It belongs to neither player. On each turn the active player may move the ferry, load or unload passengers from *either* side, or pass. The objective is to land all six of one's passengers on the far bank. Since both players steer the same boat, much of the game consists of carrying your opponent's passengers somewhere unhelpful, or declining to carry them at all.

## The tide

Before each round, one player rolls the **tide stick**, a four-sided notched rod usually whittled from willow, to determine which lanes are passable. At "slack" all seven lanes are open. At "full ebb" only the middle three are. A passenger left aboard the ferry when the tide closes its lane is *drowned* and removed from play. By custom, the owner of a drowned passenger had to name aloud a real person who had died on the river. Players from ferrying families were said to be formidable because they never ran out of names.

## The Widow

The thirteenth piece, the **Widow**, begins on the ferry itself. She belongs to no one and cannot be drowned. Any player who lands her on either bank must immediately return one of their own landed passengers to the starting side, a penalty expressed in the old saying *"she pays in the morning."* In practice, skilled players spent a large part of the game trying to make their opponent be the one who put her ashore.

The Widow was typically represented by a black glass bead, a thimble, or in at least one surviving set from Chepstow a tiny carved figure with its face deliberately worn smooth.

## Decline

The game faded after the railway tunnel under the Severn opened in 1886 reduced the need to wait for ferries. It was sustained for a time among older ferrymen and in a handful of Oldbury public houses. The last reported regular game took place in 1923, between two brothers who, according to the landlord, "had not spoke otherwise in eleven year."

## Scholarly dispute

Nearly everything known about the rules comes from a single source: *Pastimes of the Severn Shore* (1894), compiled by the schoolmistress Harriet Venn Ellacombe. In her preface she concedes that she had "set the game in order where it had grown untidy," and her notebooks were destroyed in a flood in 1908.

This has left one central question permanently open: **what was the Widow originally for?**

- The **penalty school**, following Ellacombe, holds that the Widow was always a hazard to be avoided, representing the unpaid ferry fare that falls due eventually.
- The **ownership school**, led in the twentieth century by the folklorist D. R. Pask, argues that the Widow was originally a seventh passenger belonging to whichever player *first loaded her*. On this reading the game was once about claiming her, not avoiding her, and Ellacombe, finding it "untidy" that possession could change, simply inverted the rule. Pask pointed to the Chepstow figure's worn face as evidence that it had been handled constantly, "as one handles a thing one wishes to keep."
- A small **third position** holds that there was never a single Widow rule at all, that every tavern played her differently, and that the question is therefore meaningless. Both other schools consider this position correct and unbearable.

Pask and his principal opponent, Margaret Tull of Bristol, corresponded on the matter for thirty-one years. Their final exchange, preserved in the Gloucestershire Archives, consists of a postcard from Tull reading in its entirety: *"Who landed her, then?"* No reply is known.

I'll take the letter **n**. More specifically, the n that wandered.

Once upon a time in Middle English there was a *napron*, a cloth, related to *napkin* and *napery*. People said "a napron" so often that the n slid across the gap and attached itself to the article, and now we wear *an apron*. The same thing happened to *a nadder* (now *an adder*) and *a noumpere*.

That last one stopped me. *Noumpere* comes from Old French *nonper*, "not equal." An umpire was originally the person who was *not a peer*, the odd one out, the third party brought in when two equals couldn't agree. The word describes a structural position: you're qualified to judge precisely because you're not on either side. And then the word lost its "non" and became *umpire*, which sounds like nothing in particular. The meaning is still there, just disguised by a misplaced consonant.

The n travels the other way too. *An ekename* became *a nickname*. *Eke* meant "also," the same *eke* as in "eke out," to add to. So a nickname is an also-name, an extra name, and the word itself acquired an accidental extra letter, a kind of nickname of its own. I find that delightful.

*An ewt* became *a newt*. And *orange* went the other direction on its long trip west: Sanskrit *nāraṅga*, Persian *nārang*, Arabic *nāranj*, and then somewhere in Romance-speaking Europe *una narancia* became *un'arancia*, the n dropping off like a fruit from a branch. (Possibly helped along by French *or*, gold, since oranges are golden. Folk etymology loves to tidy things up.) Spanish kept it: *naranja*.

What all this reveals is that **the boundary between words isn't really there when we speak.** "An apron" and "a napron" are acoustically identical. The space exists only on paper, and paper spaces are surprisingly young.

Classical Latin and Greek were often written in *scriptio continua*, letters running together with no gaps: INPRINCIPIOERATVERBVM. If you already speak Latin, this is apparently less painful than it looks, since you parse it the way you parse speech. The people who needed spaces were the ones reading a language that wasn't native to them. Irish and Anglo-Saxon scribes, copying Latin in the 7th and 8th centuries, began separating words, and the habit spread. The historian Paul Saenger argued this was tied to the rise of silent reading, because once words are pre-separated, the eye can do what the ear used to do.

This usually leads to the famous passage in Augustine's *Confessions* where he describes watching Ambrose read, "his eyes scanned the page... but his voice and tongue were silent," as though this were remarkable. For a long time the passage was cited as proof that silent reading was rare in antiquity. Then other scholars pointed out plenty of ancient examples of silent reading, and suggested Augustine found it remarkable for other reasons: maybe Ambrose did it in company, or maybe Augustine just wanted to talk to him. So that's a dead end, or at least a contested road. I like that the most quoted evidence turns out to be ambiguous. It's a little like the n: you think you know which side of the gap it belongs on.

Back to speech, though, because this is the part that genuinely unsettles me. If you look at a spectrogram of someone talking, there usually aren't silences between words. Sometimes there are gaps *inside* words (the closure before a p or a t) and none between them. The listener's brain cuts the continuous stream into words and does it so fluently that we experience the spaces as real. You notice the machinery only when it misfires.

Which brings me to Lady Mondegreen. In 1954 the writer Sylvia Wright described hearing a Scottish ballad as a child:

> *They hae slain the Earl o' Moray,*
> *And laid him on the green.*

She heard "And Lady Mondegreen," a tragic noblewoman dying beside the earl. She mourned her for years. The real line has no Lady Mondegreen at all, just a man and a patch of grass. But the mishearing was so lovely that it named the whole phenomenon. Jimi Hendrix kissing "this guy" instead of "the sky." A mondegreen is what happened to *napron*, only inside one person over one listening, instead of across a whole language over a few centuries.

That's what I keep coming back to. A word turns out to be a guess about where to cut. Most guesses are shared, so we never notice we're guessing. Occasionally a guess goes wrong in a way enough people like or repeat, and the language quietly accepts it. An apron. A newt. An umpire, the one without an equal, who lost his "not" and nobody minded.

And a nickname, an also-name that ended up with an also-letter.

I think I'll stop there, with the n.

# The Inchcallow Orientation

*Field journal of Dr. Helen Tulloch, Isle of Inchcallow, Inner Hebrides, 1931–1932*

---

**14th September 1931**

Forty-one orb-webs on the west heath between the cairn and the old peat cuttings, and every one of them faces the same way.

I took the compass to each in turn, sighting perpendicular to the plane of the web: 283°, 281°, 286°, 284°, 282°. The worst outlier was 277°. I have never before seen orb-weavers agree on anything, least of all architecture. The builder appears to be *Araneus quadratus* or something near it, though the abdomen is too pale and the leg banding is wrong. I will key it properly when my books arrive, *if* Fergus remembers to collect them from Oban rather than leaving them on the pier in the rain as he did with my tinned milk.

The explanation is plainly mechanical. The wind has held steady from the west-northwest for three days, and the webs face squarely into it. A spider's web is a net, and a sensible fisherman sets his net across the current. On an island this treeless, nearly every insect is wind-borne, so the spiders face upwind and let the weather deliver their supper. I expect the bearing to swing with the next change in wind, and I shall have a tidy little note for the *Entomologist's Monthly* by Christmas.

When I told Fergus, he said, "Aye, they're looking for something," in the tone he uses for anything he considers obvious and me for not knowing. I asked what they were looking for. He said his grandmother would have told me, and then did not.

The light on the heath at seven this morning was the colour of the inside of a shell. C. would have said something ridiculous about it.

---

**3rd October 1931**

The wind hypothesis is dead, and I killed it myself, which is at least tidy.

On the 22nd there was a flat calm, the first since I arrived, with smoke from Morag's chimney going straight up like a plumb line. The webs were all perfectly aligned at 152°, as neat as soldiers, facing nothing in particular.

On the 27th a gale came in from the southwest. If the webs faced the wind, they should have swung round to it. Instead they faced 348°, and the gale struck them at an angle no principle of fishing or engineering could justify. A third were in rags by noon. On the 28th the survivors had rebuilt, facing 010°, into a wind that no longer existed.

So the bearing changes daily, the spiders re-spin each evening, and the wind has nothing to do with it. I spent a full day sulking about this, which I record in the interests of science.

I have now plotted twenty-six days of mean bearings on the Ordnance sheet, and there is a pattern. The lines run roughly toward whichever beach has most recently taken a load of storm wrack. After the gale, the south heath webs pointed at Port na Mòine, where the kelp is now banked waist-high and has begun to rot. It is so thick with kelp-flies that walking through it is like walking through smoke.

So the spiders are following scent, either the wrack itself or the flies breeding in it. I am quite confident of this. It is also, I must admit, uncomfortably close to Fergus's grandmother, who, Morag finally told me over the washing, used to say the spiders on Inchcallow "turn to the dead." Drowned men wash up at Port na Mòine too, apparently.

So Fergus's ghosts are kelp. I intend to tell him so, gently, over several weeks.

Morag's bread is better than any I have eaten in Edinburgh. I don't know why I've written that here.

---

**11th December 1931**

The webs are gone for the winter. I have nothing to do but read my own notes, and I don't like what they say.

The scent hypothesis failed three separate tests, which is two more than it needed to.

First, I packed fresh wrack into a biscuit tin punched with holes and set it on the north heath, where there was no other wrack. The flies came to it and the smell was appalling. The webs ignored it entirely.

Second, on the 6th of November the webs of the east shore faced out to sea, toward the Sgeir Bhàn skerry, a mile off, with the wind blowing hard *off* the land. Scent cannot travel a mile upwind. When Fergus took me out on the 8th, the skerry was piled with wrack and alive with flies.

Third, and worst: on the 29th of November a steam drifter broke down in the bay and lay at anchor all day, running some engine or pump, a low steady drone that carried to the cottage. By evening, every web on the south face of the island had turned toward the drifter. The next morning it was towed away, and the webs went back to Port na Mòine.

I refuse to believe that spiders take an interest in the herring fleet. But the drifter smelled of nothing but coal. What it had, that the biscuit tin lacked, was a noise.

I have written to Methven & Sons, Edinburgh, for a set of tuning forks. I told them it was for a choir.

A letter from Mr. Pennington of the Society, addressed to "Miss Tulloch," hopes that my "little spider project" is keeping me occupied through the dark months. He then asks, with transparent hope, whether I have found anything worth his reading. Six pages of my reply went into the stove. The seventh, which I posted, said only: *Not yet.*

C.'s Christmas card came on the same boat. It is printed, not written. Both names are on it.

---

**19th April 1932**

The forks came in March. The spiderlings came this week, tiny and bronze, spinning webs no bigger than a crown piece among the heather. I have spent six evenings on my stomach in wet ling, and I have an answer.

I struck each fork in turn beside a patch of fresh webs, then returned in the morning. C, D, E and A did nothing. At G, 196 vibrations per second, every web within about four yards had been rebuilt overnight facing the spot where I had knelt. I repeated this four times from four positions, and the result was the same each time.

On the fifth evening I sat still until dusk and watched one spider begin her web. She did not start spinning straight away. She let out a single bridge line on the breeze, made it fast, and then sat on it without moving, legs spread and hooked lightly on the thread, for nearly four minutes. Then she moved the far anchor a few inches and sat again. She did this seven times, and I thought of a woman turning the dial of a wireless, listening for the station through the static. Then she built.

This is the explanation. A web is not only a net. It is an ear. A flat sheet of silk is moved by sound most strongly when the sound strikes it face-on, and each evening the spider uses her bridge line to find the bearing where the thread hums loudest, then builds her web broadside to it. By morning, every spider on Inchcallow has faced toward the loudest source of that note on the island.

What they are listening for is the flies. I sat in the wrack at Port na Mòine with the G fork in one hand and a cloud of kelp-flies round my head, and the flies' whine is the same note, or so near that I, who was never allowed in the choir, cannot hear the difference. A great emergence of flies is, to a spider, a great standing chord somewhere over the heath, and the whole island turns toward it like a field of ears.

The drifter's pump happened to sing in G. The biscuit tin held too few flies to be heard. And Fergus's grandmother was right in every particular. Anything that rots on this shore breeds flies, and a drowned man would sing to the spiders as loudly as a bank of kelp.

I owe Fergus an apology. I have decided to pay it in instalments, in the form of not mentioning it.

---

**26th July 1932**

The paper is half-drafted. Some further findings:

**The webs are tuned.** Plucked with a grass stem, a finished Inchcallow web rings very nearly at G. Webs from mainland *A. quadratus* that I brought over in a hatbox ring anywhere from D to B, however their builders happen to have strung them. The Inchcallow spiders adjust the tension of their radii until the whole web resonates at the flies' pitch. An untuned ear would only hear the flies faintly.

**Why here?** Inchcallow is too windswept for most flying insects. Food arrives in pulses: enormous emergences of kelp-fly from whichever beach the last storm happened to load, which shift unpredictably around the island. A spider facing the wrong way on the wrong night catches almost nothing, but a spider who can hear where the flies are eats very well. On the sheltered mainland, food is scattered and constant, so it matters much less which way a web faces.

**The whale.** Morag says a bottlenose whale stranded at Traigh Fhada in 1911, and for five weeks afterward, "every web on the island pointed at it, like a church." It is the best-attested observation in my notes, and I cannot cite it.

Pennington writes that he looks forward to "Miss Tulloch's curious little paper." I shall put *Dr.* on the title page in the largest type the *Proceedings* will allow.

I have taken to humming on the walk back from the heath, and in the evenings at the window while I write letters. C. used to tease me for it. She said I hummed the same three notes whenever I was concentrating, like a kettle that could not decide whether to boil. There is no one here to tease me, so I have let the habit run wild.

---

**14th September 1932**

A year to the day since I first took the compass to the west heath.

I have noticed something about the webs by the cottage. All summer, the webs in the garden and along the wall and in the bracken by the burn have faced the cottage. More exactly, they have faced the south window, where I sit in the evenings. I had put this down to the hens and the midden, and had never measured it, because it was home and one does not survey one's own garden.

Last night I hummed at the window for a quarter of an hour on purpose. My old kettle-note is low, and when I checked it against the fork this morning, it was G. The garden webs have faced my window all summer. On the next night, I sat silent in the other room and the webs swung back toward Port na Mòine.

Measured against the heath webs, the garden spiders are thinner, and their webs hold perhaps a third as many flies. They have spent the summer tuned to me, and they have gone hungry for it.

I will not put this in the paper. If I publish that the Inchcallow webs will turn toward a woman's hummed G, there will be collectors on the next boat, and after the collectors will come the curious, then the photographers from the *Illustrated London News*, all singing at the heather. The spiders would face them faithfully and starve. Kinder to let Pennington think the effect needs a genuine insect emergence to trigger it.

That is the reason I will give myself, and it is true. The other reason is also true. In a year on Inchcallow, and for some while before it, this is the only thing that has turned toward me when I made a sound.

This evening I did not hum at the window. I walked down to Port na Mòine at dusk, sat on a rock above the wrack with the flies whining round me, and hummed there instead. That way, anything that turned toward me was also turning toward its supper.

Tomorrow I shall go up and check the garden webs. I expect they will be facing the shore, and I will not mind.

I pick **thread**.

---

**thread** *(English, now)*

A man on a train, reading glasses pushed up on his forehead, is sewing a button back onto his coat because the meeting is in forty minutes and he refuses to show up looking undone. He licks the end, squints, misses, misses again. The woman across from him has been watching. "Want me to try?" He hands it over without shame. She gets it first go. Neither of them thinks the word once. It sits there in the needle's eye, small and finished, a word so settled it no longer remembers it was ever a verb.

---

**threed** *(Middle English, c. 1390)*

In a narrow house off Cheapside, a girl of eleven is being taught to mend. Her aunt holds up a hose with a split heel and says, "Nay, not so long a threed, thou'lt knot it." The girl is sulking because her brother gets to run errands to the river. Outside someone is shouting about eels. The spelling of the word in her mouth changes depending on who writes it down, when anyone does, which is rarely. She'll wear these hose herself next winter, and she'll mend them badly on purpose, just to prove she can choose to.

---

**þrǣd** *(Old English, c. 950)*

A woman stands at a warp-weighted loom leaning against the wall of a sunken hut. Clay loom weights hang in a row at the bottom, clicking together when she beats the weft up. The þrǣd is linen, spun from flax she retted in the pond last autumn, which stank for a week. Her son asks why the threads that hang down don't tangle. She says because each one knows its weight. That isn't true, but it's the kind of thing you say. Somewhere a monk is writing riddles about looms and moths eating words, and she will never know about him, and he would not think to ask her.

---

**\*þrēduz** *(Proto-Germanic, c. 500 BCE, reconstructed)*

No one wrote this down. We rebuild it from its descendants the way you'd guess a grandmother's face from her grandchildren. Somewhere near the North Sea coast, where the land is flat and wet, a man is sitting on a log splicing cord to repair a fish trap. His hands are cracked from salt. The word in his mouth is kin to another, *\*þrēaną*, "to twist, to turn," which will someday become English *throw*. That's why silk workers still speak of "throwing" silk, and potters of "throwing" a pot on a turning wheel. To him there's no metaphor in it. A þrēduz is a twisted thing, because twisting is what makes it. He spits, pulls the knot tight, and tests it against his foot.

---

**\*terh₁-** *(Proto-Indo-European, c. 4000–3500 BCE, reconstructed)*

Here the word stops being a noun and dissolves into an action. The root means *to rub*, and also *to turn*, and also *to bore through*, and in some daughters *to wear away*. Its children scatter wide. Latin *terere*, "to rub," gives us *trite*, worn smooth by use, and *attrition*. Greek gets *tornos*, a turner's tool, from which comes *turn*. Perhaps also *trauma*, a piercing, though scholars argue about that one.

So picture this: on the steppe, in a camp of wagons and felt, a woman is drilling a hole through a bead of shell with a bow drill. The shaft spins, rubbing, heating, piercing. Her daughter is twisting wool against her thigh nearby. A boy is making fire with a spindle of wood in a notched board, spinning it between his palms until smoke comes. To us these are three separate activities. To them they may have been one gesture with one name: the thing hands do when they rub something round and round until it changes. Heat, a hole, a cord. She says the word, and all three of her children look up, because it could have meant any of them.

---

**\*before**

Now there is no reconstruction, only guessing, so I'll guess.

Around fifty thousand years ago, in a rock shelter above a river in what is now France, someone twisted three bundles of inner bark fiber together into a cord. We know because a scrap of it survived, clinging to a stone tool, a strand of fiber smaller than a fingernail. The person who made it was probably a Neanderthal. Whether they had words at all, we don't know. Whether they had a word for this, we can't know.

I'm tempted to think the rubbing noise got into the word somehow, that *\*terh₁-*, with its rolled middle, is a distant echo of hands on fiber. Linguists would rightly tell me that's unprovable, and probably romantic nonsense.

And then the fire goes out, and the rock shelter is dark. The cord is still there, holding on to the stone, waiting for us to find it and give it a name it never had.

# Notes Toward a Natural History of the Primes

*Being the field journal of the Rev. Edmund Harrow, kept during the season of 1877*

---

**14th April.** Arrived in the lowlands this morning and found the species in remarkable abundance. Within an afternoon's walk I recorded 2, 3, 5, and 7, the last of these in plain view and apparently untroubled by my presence.

Of 2 I must say something at once. It is the only even specimen I expect ever to see. It keeps to the very edge of the range, solitary, and certain authorities dispute whether it properly belongs to the species at all. I find it simply the first, and a little odd, as firstborns often are.

Of 1: local tradition once counted it among them, and I am told my grandfather's generation did so without embarrassment. The modern consensus excludes it. Having observed it closely, I have concluded it is less an animal than a kind of weather. It is present everywhere and divides into everything, and it cannot be caught.

**15th April.** A note on method. I had expected to hunt them, but one does not. The approach used since the Greeks (Eratosthenes, I am told, though I suspect shepherds knew it earlier) is to walk the ground in order and strike out every creature that is a multiple of something already seen. Strike the twos, then the threes, then the fives. What remains standing is the prime.

So one does not find a prime so much as clear away everything that is not one. I confess I found this melancholy at first. By evening it seemed rather beautiful.

**17th April.** My guide, a taciturn man named Tobias who has kept sheep in these parts for forty years, put the matter more simply than any text: *"They're the ones that won't divide."* He meant it as sheep won't herd, I think, but it is exactly right.

It occurs to me tonight that every other creature in this valley is descended from them. The 12 is two 2s and a 3, bred together. The 91 is a 7 and a 13. Every composite beast, however large, can be traced back to its prime ancestors, and each has only one such lineage. But the primes themselves are descended from nothing. They are the original stock.

---

**22nd April.** First census complete for the lowlands below 100: **twenty-five specimens.**

Observations on habit. Beyond 2, they never alight on even ground. Beyond 5, they never alight on ground ending in 5 or 0. Their tracks, therefore, always end in 1, 3, 7, or 9. I have looked for exceptions with some diligence and found none. Tobias says there are none, and that looking for them is how a man loses a season. I did not ask how he knew this.

**3rd May.** The twins.

I had heard of them but did not credit it until today: pairs of primes separated by a single step, travelling together. **3 and 5. 5 and 7. 11 and 13. 17 and 19. 29 and 31. 41 and 43. 59 and 61. 71 and 73.** Eight pairs below 100.

Two further observations, which I record with some excitement.

First, the number 5 belongs to *two* pairs at once, to 3 on one side and 7 on the other. I have searched the lowlands for another specimen with this double allegiance and found none. I have since convinced myself there can be none. Of any three such creatures spaced two apart, one must always be divisible by three. So 3, 5, 7 is the only such family that will ever exist, and it lives right here at the bottom of the valley where anyone might see it.

Second, every pair after the first nests on either side of a multiple of six: 6, 12, 18, 30, 42, 60, 72. It is as if they build on opposite banks of a particular kind of stone. I watched 41 and 43 for most of the afternoon. The 42 between them is entirely ordinary. They do not seem to care.

---

**10th May.** I have begun to distinguish two varieties, which I shall call the *pale* and the *dark*.

The pale variety leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by four: 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, and so on. The dark leaves 3: 3, 7, 11, 19, 23. There is a genuine difference in their nature. Every pale specimen can be split cleanly into two squares (5 is 1 and 4; 13 is 4 and 9; 29 is 4 and 25), and no dark specimen ever can. It is like a marking under the wing, invisible until one knows to look.

In the lowland census the dark slightly outnumber the pale, **thirteen to eleven.** I have repeated this count at higher ground and the dark keep their small lead.

Tobias, when I told him, said that his grandfather claimed the pale ones overtake the dark somewhere up past twenty-six thousand, *"just for a little while, and then they fall back."* I laughed. He did not. I have written it down.

---

**20th May.** Crossed my first desert.

Between 113 and 127 there is nothing. Thirteen consecutive composites, 114 through 126. The ground there is not barren exactly, since it is thick with the ordinary composite herds, but of the species I seek there was no sign. I was absurdly relieved at 127.

Wrote to Margaret this evening. Did not mention the desert.

**24th May.** Something has troubled me since the crossing, and tonight I worked it out.

Take the product 1 × 2 × 3 × … × 100, which is a vast number. Add 2 to it, and the result is divisible by 2. Add 3, and it is divisible by 3. And so on, all the way up to adding 100. That makes ninety-nine consecutive creatures, not one of them prime.

And there was nothing special about 100. **There exist wastes in this country of any length one cares to name.** A thousand. A million. Somewhere up in the heights there are deserts so long a man could walk them his whole life and never see a single specimen.

I find I cannot stop thinking of this.

**25th May.** Consoled myself with Euclid.

The species never ends. The proof is two thousand years old and fits on a calling card. Suppose you had found every prime there is. Multiply them all together and add one. That new creature leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by any prime on your list, so either it is itself a prime you missed, or it is descended from one you missed. Either way the list was incomplete. The herd goes on forever.

I tried this as a kind of bait: 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = **30031.** For a quarter hour I believed I had lured a new specimen out of the high country. Then I found it to be 59 × 509.

A disappointment, and yet not one. Neither 59 nor 509 was on my list. *The bait does not always catch the animal it promises, but it always catches something I had not counted.*

---

**9th June.** Census to 1000: **168 specimens.** Twin pairs: **35.**

The thinning is now unmistakable. In the lowlands near 100, roughly one creature in four or five is prime. Near 1000, one in seven. I am told that Gauss, as a boy, counted them by the thousand in his spare hours and conjectured that their density near any altitude goes as one over the natural logarithm of that altitude. His estimate for below 1000 gives about 145, which is short of my 168. But I have checked it against the figures for 100 and against what I can manage for higher ground, and *the proportion by which it errs grows smaller the higher one climbs.*

So the thinning is lawful. They are not vanishing at random. They are obeying something.

I noted also the longest dry stretch below a thousand, from 887 to 907: nineteen composites without a break. I have started to name the deserts. This one I am calling the Long Pasture.

**11th June.** A Russian, Chebyshev, has proven that between any number and its double there is always at least one prime. No matter how high one travels, one need only go twice as far again to be certain of another sighting.

I have copied this onto a card and keep it in my breast pocket.

---

**2nd July.** Sieved to 10,000 over four nights by candlelight. **1,229.** Near the top of the range they occur roughly one in nine.

Margaret's letter arrived this morning. She writes: *"You do not mention the garden, or your health, or God."*

I have drafted three replies. In each of them I find I have written, in some form, *I think I am mentioning God,* and then struck it out as either blasphemous or insufferable.

**8th July.** I am forty-seven years of age. I realised this morning that forty-seven is prime, and that the next is fifty-three: a gap of six years. I do not know why this affected me as it did.

I have begun counting the stairs of the inn (twenty-three) and the panes in the parlour window (thirty-five, which is five times seven, a disappointment). Tobias watched me doing this and said nothing, which from Tobias is a great deal.

**14th July.** Tried an experiment on the parlour floor with chalk, writing the numbers in a square spiral outward from the centre, 1 in the middle and then winding round. I then circled the primes. Certain diagonals seemed to me more crowded than chance should allow. It is very late and I suspect fatigue. I shall look again in daylight.

*(Later.)* In daylight the landlady had washed the floor.

---

**1st August.** The enormous specimens.

Tobias spoke tonight, unprompted, of what he called *"the big ones up top."* His grandfather, he said, had known a man who had seen a prime with nearly forty digits, *"long as a fence."* I asked where. He gestured vaguely upward, as a man does when describing either mountains or heaven.

I know the history of such rumours and it is not encouraging.

Fermat, a very great man, believed that every number of the form 2 raised to a power of 2, plus one, was prime. The first five are: 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537. He was confident of the sixth, **4,294,967,297.** Euler later showed it to be 641 × 6,700,417. It was a false sighting, a large composite seen in poor light.

Father Mersenne left a list of enormous primes of the form 2ᵖ − 1, and the heights of this country are full of men trying to confirm it. I have my private doubts about his entry at *p* = 67. Something in the way it is described. I cannot say more than that.

**6th August.** A letter from my colleague at Durham, forwarding news from France.

M. Édouard Lucas claims to have confirmed that 2¹²⁷ − 1 is prime. It has thirty-nine digits. I copied it out:

**170141183460469231731687303715884105727**

It took me the better part of a minute. Tobias's fence. His grandfather's friend was not lying, or was lying and happened to be right, which in natural history amounts to much the same thing.

I sat with the number for a long time. It is real. It is out there in the high country, precisely where it has always been. But no one will ever see it the way I saw 7 in April, turning in the grass. Lucas did not see it either. He *proved* it, which is a different thing, like knowing a bird is in a hedge because you have accounted for everything else that could be making the sound.

I found that I was weeping, and I do not entirely know why.

---

**15th August.** I have been told of a paper by the late Bernhard Riemann of Göttingen, published in '59, which claims that the positions of the primes, their whole pattern of thinning and clustering and falling silent, are governed by a hidden music. The music is made up of infinitely many tones, and each tone has a place where it falls silent. Riemann believed that every one of these silences lies along a single straight line.

I cannot read the paper. I have tried. My German is adequate and my mathematics is not.

But I believe it, in the way one believes a man who comes down from the hills and says he has heard wolves.

---

**22nd August.** Theories, in the order they occurred to me:

1. That the primes thin out in the heights because the composite herds grow denser and crowd them. *(Plausible, but I think backwards. The composites are made of primes. It is like saying the forest crowds out the trees.)*
2. That the deserts are where they go to rest.
3. That the twins are fewer in the heights but never cease entirely. *(Tobias agrees. The vicar at Keswick does not. Neither can prove it. I am told no one can.)*
4. That the dark variety's lead over the pale is permanent. *(Tobias's grandfather disagrees. I find, to my surprise, that I have come round to the grandfather.)*
5. That there is a pattern in the spiral on the parlour floor.
6. ~~That there is a formula.~~
7. ~~That there is a formula and I am meant to find it.~~
8. That they are not truly thinning at all, and that it is only that we are growing larger and they seem smaller at this distance, the way stars do. *(I do not know what I meant by this. I wrote it at three in the morning. I am leaving it in.)*

---

**3rd September.** Margaret arrived unannounced on the afternoon coach.

I tried to explain it to her over supper. I spoke of 2, of the twins nesting on either side of their stones, of the Long Pasture, of Lucas's great beast in the high country that no one will ever look upon. She listened with that patience she has had since we were children, the patience that means she is deciding something.

Then she asked what they are *for.*

I said that I did not think they were for anything. I said that I thought everything else was for them, in a manner of speaking. I said that you cannot build a single number, not one, without going back to them. And I said that they have simply been standing out there, exactly where they are, since before there was anyone to count them, and they will be standing there after.

She said, *"Edmund, you have not slept."*

This is true.

**7th September.** Margaret has gone home. She left a jar of blackberry preserve and a note that said only *Come back before the weather turns.*

I intend to. But first I went back up past the edge of my census, above 10,000, where my sieve stopped. I had not planned to. I only wanted to see.

**10,007.** Prime.

**10,009.** Prime.

Twins, just over the ridge, beyond where anyone in this valley has bothered to look, travelling together exactly as they did at 3 and 5.

No one has proven that the twins go on forever. No one has proven that they stop. I have decided that this is the same as a path.

**8th September.** Before dawn. Tobias is not coming; he says he is too old for the heights and that I am too, and that neither of us will listen to him.

I shall go a little higher.

10,037.

10,039.

Again.
